items.descriptionOriginal: You've recorded a video you can't wait to share. But before anyone sees it, you have to trim clips, choose music, add subtitles, and maybe even dub it into another language. Suddenly, something that took a few minutes to film can turn into hours of work. If you've ever made an Instagram reel, a college video or even a birthday montage, you probably know how frustrating this can get. Now imagine doing it for a living, often without a team of editors or the money for expensive tools. For young creators with plenty of ideas but limited resources, turning those ideas into videos people will enjoy watching can be a real challenge. Arjun Sai's AatonovaZ brings filming, editing and multilingual dubbing together in one AI-powered ecosystem. But what if you could simply tell a drone what to film, ask AI to edit the footage and have your video dubbed into another language, all through voice commands? That's exactly what 21-year-old Kosinepalli Arjun Sai from Tirupati is working towards. A graduate in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning from Mohan Babu University, Arjun has built AatonovaZ Technologies Pvt Ltd, a student-led startup developing AI-powered tools that aim to make filming, editing and dubbing videos easier for creators, especially those working on their own. A Telugu version of Swades sparked his first AI idea The idea began with a film Arjun wanted to watch, long before he started working on drones and other AI systems. During his first semester of engineering in 2023, Arjun wanted to watch Swades , the acclaimed film starring Shah Rukh Khan. However, he struggled to find a Telugu-dubbed version. "I don't understand native Hindi that well," Arjun explains. "I wanted to watch the film in Telugu, but I couldn't find a version. When I researched further, I realised there was no simple way to do it without a dubbing studio and high costs." That discovery gave Arjun the idea for JusDub, an AI-powered multilingual dubbing tool that would later become part of AatonovaZ, the startup he founded. But as he explored the problem further, he realised that dubbing was only one part of a much longer process. Why did creators need so many different tools to shoot, edit and share a single video? Arjun's first idea came from struggling to find a Telugu-dubbed version of Shah Rukh Khan's film Swades. Creators typically shoot using one device, edit using another platform, generate audio elsewhere, and then use separate tools for translation or dubbing. Arjun felt there had to be a more seamless way. "We saw creators juggling multiple tools just to bring one idea to life," he says. "We wanted to create a system where you simply come with your idea, your voice and your intent, and the ecosystem handles everything else." That vision eventually grew into AatonovaZ, an AI ecosystem designed to support creators from production to distribution. One startup, three tools to make a video Unlike standalone editing software or generative AI applications, AatonovaZ combines multiple technologies into a single workflow. The startup currently revolves around three flagship products: GarudaOne – A smart drone that can film videos when you give it simple voice instructions, such as "follow me" or "take a 360-degree shot". Editra – An AI video editor that takes your raw footage, puts the clips together, adds music and transitions, and prepares an edited video for you. JusDub – An AI dubbing tool that translates videos into different languages while trying to preserve the speaker's emotions, whether they're happy, excited or sad. GarudaOne is designed to let creators direct drone footage using voice commands in Indian languages, including Hindi and Telugu. Together, these tools aim to bring tasks usually handled by videographers, editors, sound designers and dubbing artists into one connected system. The company describes this approach as a "cyber-physical ecosystem", which essentially means bringing physical devices and AI-powered software together so they can work as one system. "Most AI today exists only inside laptops or data centres," Arjun explains. "Our drone is a physical AI system. It takes decisions, performs obstacle avoidance, understands commands and coordinates with cloud-based software. Multiple systems work together seamlessly through AI. " The concept has attracted attention because it merges physical hardware and generative AI into a creator-focused workflow rather than treating them as separate technologies. A drone that can take filming commands in Hindi & Telugu Among AatonovaZ's products, GarudaOne is perhaps the most futuristic. Instead of requiring users to manually control a drone through joysticks or complicated flight settings, the system is designed to respond to natural voice instructions. A creator wearing a microphone can issue commands such as "orbit me", "zoom in", or "take a 360-degree shot", and the drone is designed to plan its flight path, avoid obstacles and capture the footage automatically. According to Arjun, one of its most striking features is multilingual compatibility. Mentorship at Mohan Babu University helped Arjun narrow down his ideas and turn them into a student-led startup. "The beauty of this drone is that it can be controlled using Indian languages," he says. "You can instruct it in Hindi, Telugu or other languages, and it understands what needs to be done." Behind the scenes, AI helps the drone understand what you're asking it to do, work out where and how to fly, avoid obstacles and share information with other connected software. Building such a system, however, has not been easy. "The biggest challenge is engineering," Arjun admits. "It's easy to say AI can do everything, but these models require significant computing power. Running powerful AI on compact hardware like a drone is one of the toughest problems we are solving." One hour of footage, edited in 20 minutes? If GarudaOne handles production, Editra is designed to handle what happens after filming. Most AI editing tools today assist creators by recommending cuts or suggesting improvements. Editra aims to go further. Arjun describes it as a system capable of understanding context, arranging footage, generating background music, adding transitions and preparing a draft version with minimal human intervention. "You bring the raw footage and we do the heavy lifting," he says. "The goal is that you upload your clips and receive a final draft ready for use." One feature the team believes could be particularly useful for creators is AI-generated, copyright-free music. "Audio has a huge impact on engagement," Arjun explains. "If the sound isn't right, the emotional connection is lost. We generate music automatically, so creators don't have to worry about copyright issues." According to Arjun, editing a typical one-hour recording using Editra can take as little as 10 to 20 minutes, depending on the video's length and the user's preferences. Creators can also incorporate additional human supervision when they want a specific editing style. Can AI dubbing preserve the emotion behind someone's words? But even after a video is edited, there's another challenge for creators who want to reach people who speak different languages. It's a problem Arjun understood personally when he couldn't find Swades in Telugu. And it's what led him to build JusDub, his first AI product and the one that remains closest to his heart. The platform addresses a challenge that millions of Indian creators encounter: producing content across multiple languages without losing emotional authenticity. Traditional text-to-speech systems can generate fluent speech but often struggle to preserve emotional expression. "The missing piece was emotion," says Arjun. "A laugh, excitement or sadness in one language often gets flattened when translated into another." Think of someone excitedly sharing good news, or a person speaking through tears. Even if their words are translated correctly, the feeling behind them can get lost when a computer-generated voice reads them out. AatonovaZ secured Rs 20 lakh in pre-seed funding under the Startup India Seed Fund Scheme to develop its technology. That's what Arjun wants to change with JusDub. He explains that the AI tool is designed to pick up emotions in the original recording and adjust the voice, speed and tone in the dubbed version to match them. For a creator making a video in Telugu, for instance, the idea is to help someone watching it in Hindi experience the same excitement, humour or sadness. And in a country where people speak so many different languages, this could help creators share their videos with more people without spending heavily on separate dubbing studios. The mentors who helped turn ideas into a startup As Arjun began working on solutions for filming, editing and dubbing, he had several ideas he wanted to explore. But figuring out which ones to pursue and how to turn them into working products was another challenge. That's where his mentors played an important role, helping him narrow down his ideas and focus on what he wanted to build. According to Yudhish Jain, who mentors student entrepreneurs through the university's incubation ecosystem, Arjun's strongest quality was his focus on understanding the problem deeply before building solutions. "Arjun and his team know their product inside out," he says. "They have gone to the market, spoken to users and understood the sentiment. Their differentiation comes from the technology and their clarity of purpose." Jain believes tools like these could make it easier for more people to start creating videos, especially those who have the talent and ideas but struggle to get started. "Many people possess skills and talent, but they don't know how to enter the creator ecosystem," he says. "What Arjun and his team are building addresses a market that remains largely untapped." Dr Padmaja and other university mentors helped Arjun refine his ideas, connect with experts and take his startup forward. For Arjun, mentorship has been equally critical. "Many founders get distracted by multiple opportunities," he says. "My mentors constantly helped me stay aligned with the vision and avoid losing focus." The university's support also opened doors for Arjun and his team. They got opportunities to connect with other entrepreneurs and learn from startup programmes, including exposure to NSRCEL at IIM Bangalore. These experiences helped them figure out how to turn their ideas into a business. From a campus idea to Rs 20 lakh in funding and global recognition Along the way, the startup also received funding and recognition for their work. AatonovaZ secured Rs 20 lakh in pre-seed funding under the Startup India Seed Fund Scheme, received support from government-backed incubators, and ranked among the Top 25 teams globally in Samsung Solve for Tomorrow. The company also won ANVESHAN 2025–26 after emerging victorious in the South Zone competition. (Organised by the Association of Indian Universities, ANVESHAN is a student research and innovation competition where university teams present ideas and inventions aimed at solving real-world problems.) For Dr Padmaja, Deputy Dean – Innovations at Mohan Babu University, these achievements show what can happen when students get the right environment and encouragement. "I still remember when Arjun came to me with nearly 10 raw ideas," she recalls. "I could see a spark in him. We connected him with mentors and provided guidance, and that changed the trajectory of the team." Still in the validation and pilot deployment stage, AatonovaZ is working towards making its connected AI tools commercially available to creators. She believes success stories like AatonovaZ have a wider impact across campus. "When students see founders among their peers, they stop asking 'Who will hire me?' and begin asking 'What can I build?' and 'How can I create opportunities for others?'" Today, AatonovaZ remains in the validation and pilot deployment stage. The company has tested its vision through multiple prototypes and is working towards commercialisation. Its larger ambition extends beyond creating individual AI tools. Arjun often compares the vision to Apple's ecosystem model, where hardware and software work together to deliver a seamless experience. "We don't just want to build tools," he says. "We want to build an experience. In simple terms, we want to create the iPhone for content creators." All images courtesy of Arjun Sai

items.descriptionOriginal: For generations, the people of Gohain Chapori in Assam's Dhemaji district have shared something special with the wildlife around them. On the same land where villagers take their cattle and buffaloes to graze, wild deer have found a home. Birds, including wild ducks, are also part of this landscape. For the families living here, sharing their surroundings with these animals has been a part of life for years. But with hunting, encroachment and other pressures threatening the habitat, villagers began thinking about what they could do to protect it. And now, four villages in Assam are coming together with an ambitious plan: to turn 1,044 bighas of shared grazing land into a village forest reserve, giving around 150 deer a safer home. What makes their effort special is that the people who depend on this land for their livelihoods also want to take responsibility for protecting its wildlife. A home for cattle, deer and everything in between The Maghuwa Hola grazing ground stretches across Gohain Chapori, Hator Khola, Puthimari and No. 1 Barmuthoni villages. Much of this government land is used for grazing cattle and buffaloes, while a small forest within it provides shelter to hog deer, wild ducks and other wildlife. But sharing land comes with challenges. Hunting poses a direct threat to the animals. Encroachment, grazing pressures and seasonal floods can also affect the places where they live. The village also hopes to explore structured ecotourism as part of the initiative. Photograph: (Chandra Mohan Patowary) And protecting the deer isn't as simple as keeping people and cattle away. Families have depended on these grazing grounds for generations, so any plan to protect wildlife must also consider their needs. That is what makes the villagers' proposal meaningful. They want to protect the animals while ensuring that the land continues to support the communities living around it. With support from the Dhemaji district administration and Forest Department, they are now working towards establishing the Maghuwa Hola Village Forest Reserve. How four villages began turning their plan into action On 2 October 2026, villagers, students, young people, women's self-help groups and government officials came together at Maghuwa Hola. And they began with something practical. Through shramadan , or voluntary community labour, they worked on an approximately one-kilometre approach road leading towards the proposed reserve. Native saplings were planted along the road. An exhibition helped people understand the deer population and conservation plans, while a signboard marked the beginning of the initiative. The community also gathered for a Gaon Sabha , or village meeting, to discuss the proposal and the steps needed to protect the land. The idea is to put the people who live closest to the forest at the centre of decisions about its future. A village-level committee is planned to help manage the area, with proposed rules against hunting, burning and encroachment. Grazing and fishing would be regulated so that people can continue using the land without putting unnecessary pressure on wildlife. As Dhemaji District Commissioner Rahul Suresh Javir told Indian Masterminds , "The reserve should begin with the people who will actually protect it." What will it take to give 150 deer a safer home? There is still some work to be done before Maghuwa Hola can officially become a village forest reserve. Because the land is already classified as a grazing reserve, the Forest and Revenue Departments must examine its boundaries, legal status and existing community rights. The proposal will then need approval from the Assam government. Villagers also hope to explore responsible ecotourism in the future, which could create earning opportunities for local families while encouraging continued protection of the area. But the most important part of this initiative has already begun: people are coming together to protect the land they share with wildlife. There is no guarantee that creating a reserve will solve every challenge. Keeping hunting and encroachment in check, protecting the habitat and balancing grazing needs will require continued cooperation. Still, the first steps offer hope. For generations, these four villages have made room for deer alongside their cattle. Now, by working together, they are trying to make sure that the next generation gets to see these animals here, too. Sources: 'In Assam's Dhemaji, Grazing Land Being Developed As Village Forest' : By Ratnadip Choudhury, Published on 4 October 2026 'In Dhemaji, Villagers Are Building a Forest Reserve for 150 Deer — And They Started With Shramadan' : By Muskan Khandelwal, Published 0n 9 October 2026

Τον Νοέμβριο του 1997, αυτό το κορίτσι, η Kalpana Chawla, κοίταξε από ψηλά τη Γη από το Διαστημικό Λεωφορείο Columbia και είπε ότι η θέα την έκανε να αισθάνεται λιγότερο σαν κάποια από ένα κομμάτι γης και περισσότερο σαν κάποια από…
items.descriptionOriginal: Long before she became the first Indian woman in space, a girl in Karnal followed her father to a local flying club and watched planes lift into the sky. In November 1997, that girl, Kalpana Chawla, looked down on Earth from Space Shuttle Columbia, and she said the view made her feel less like someone from one patch of land and more like someone from the solar system. Her journey set a template that many people with Indian roots have followed since, in orbit, in laboratories, in hospitals and in the rooms where global institutions decide how the world should run. Most of them now carry another country's passport. But for people like them, India created the Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) card, a lifelong link to the country their families came from. This list gathers 10 changemakers, five women and five men, who fit that description and were chosen for work that served the world rather than personal fortune. But what does OCI mean? OCI is a lifelong, multiple-entry visa for people of Indian origin who hold another country's citizenship. It is not dual citizenship: cardholders cannot vote or hold constitutional posts, but they can live and work in India indefinitely. Anyone who was, or was eligible to become, an Indian citizen on or after 26 January 1950, and their descendants, can apply. Kalpana Chawla, the astronaut who flew first Born in Karnal in 1962, Chawla became the first Indian woman in space aboard Space Shuttle Columbia in 1997. Chawla's journey from Karnal to NASA continues to inspire young Indians, particularly girls, to pursue careers in science and aerospace. Photograph: ( Asian American Historical Society ) She died on 1 February, 2003 when Columbia broke up on re-entry, having logged 30 days, 14 hours, and 54 minutes in space. The US Congress awarded her its Space Medal of Honor posthumously, and a cargo spacecraft launched to the International Space Station in October 2020 carried her name. Abhijit Banerjee, the economist who tested poverty Banerjee studied at the University of Calcutta and Jawaharlal Nehru University before earning his doctorate at Harvard. He won the 2019 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences for an experimental approach to alleviating poverty, built on randomised controlled trials. He co-founded the Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab in 2003, and he shared the Nobel with Esther Duflo and Michael Kremer. Sunita Williams, the record-setting spacewalker Williams, whose father hails from Gujarat, received the Padma Bhushan in 2008. She completed nine spacewalks totalling 62 hours and 6 minutes, the most by any woman, and retired from NASA on 27 December, 2025 after 608 days in space. On earlier missions, she carried a Ganesha idol and samosas, a reminder of her heritage. Venkatraman Ramakrishnan, the chemist who mapped the ribosome Born in Chidambaram in 1952, Ramakrishnan shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for mapping the ribosome, the cellular machinery that builds proteins. Understanding the ribosome's structure has helped researchers investigate how antibiotics interact with bacteria and how resistance can develop. Photograph: ( TNM ) That structure has proved important in the production of antibiotics. He studied physics at Baroda University before moving to the United States for his doctorate. Gita Gopinath, the economist who broke an IMF barrier Born in Kolkata in 1971, Gopinath became the first woman to serve as chief economist of the International Monetary Fund in October 2018. She later served as its first deputy managing director from 2022 to 2025 before returning to Harvard. She studied at Delhi University before earning her PhD at Princeton in 2001. Atul Gawande, the surgeon behind a checklist Gawande led the World Health Organization effort behind the surgical safety checklist , tested in eight hospitals worldwide, from a major academic centre in the United States to a rural facility in Tanzania. A study published in January 2009 found that major complications fell by 36% and deaths by 47%, with in-hospital mortality falling from 1.5% to 0.8%. Priyamvada Natarajan, the astrophysicist who maps dark matter Born in Coimbatore and raised in Delhi, Natarajan teaches at Yale. Her work on dark matter and black holes earned her a place on Time's 2024 list of the 100 most influential people and the 2025 Dannie Heineman Prize in Astrophysics. Natarajan's research explores how supermassive black holes form and how dark matter shapes the universe's large-scale structure. Photograph: ( Deccan Herald ) Her proposed pathway for forming black hole seeds in the early universe has since been supported by data from the James Webb Space Telescope. Vivek Murthy, the Surgeon General who named loneliness As US Surgeon General, Murthy issued an advisory on 2 May, 2023 warning that loneliness and isolation had become a major public health concern for Americans. He had earlier testified before the US Senate Finance Committee on youth mental health care, on 8 February, 2022. Indra Nooyi, the executive who tied profit to purpose Born in Chennai in 1955, Nooyi led PepsiCo from 2006 to 2018 and was the first woman of colour and immigrant to head a Fortune 50 company. Her Performance with Purpose strategy linked growth to healthier products, and India honoured her with the Padma Bhushan in 2007. She stepped down as chief executive in October 2018 and as chairman in early 2019. Sudhir Parikh, the doctor who served communities Parikh, a Gujarat-born doctor based in the United States, won the Pravasi Bharatiya Samman in 2006 and received the Padma Shri in 2010 for social service. Alongside his medical career, Parikh has supported social causes, earning recognition from both the Indian and Indian diaspora communities. Photograph: ( India.com ) He is also known for his expertise in treating asthma and allergies. Why these stories matter Read together, these 10 lives cover remarkable ground, from the silence of orbit to the operating theatres where a checklist cut deaths by 47%, and from the protein factory inside a cell to the daily choices of a poor family. India has honoured several of them, with Padma awards going to Williams, Nooyi and Parikh, yet each story reaches beyond any award because the work itself serves people far from where it began. Chawla carried a childhood fascination with planes and flight into orbit, Banerjee turned poverty into a question that experiments could answer, and Ramakrishnan turned the structure of proteins into a map that doctors can use today. Their stories remind us how a connection to India can travel across continents and still carry the same wish to help people beyond one country, all with an OCI card. Sources ' Sunita Williams retires from NASA after 27 years, three missions and record 608 days in space ': by IANS for IANS Live, Published on 21 January, 2026 ' Kalpana Chawla: Biography & Columbia disaster ': by Nola Taylor Tillman for Space.com ' Abhijit Banerjee, Esther Duflo, and Michael Kremer Awarded Nobel Prize in 2019 for Research on Economic Development ': by NBER for National Bureau of Economic Research ' The checklist manifesto: how to get things right ': by PubMed Central ' Venkatraman Ramakrishnan, Facts ': by Nobel Prize Outreach for NobelPrize.org

items.title: Σκουλήκια και μια παρατεταμένη δυσωδία: Τι μπορεί να έχει προκαλέσει το θάνατο των ψαριών της λίμνης Doddagubbi
items.titleOriginal: Maggots and a Lingering Stench: What May Have Caused Doddagubbi Lake’s Fish Kill
items.description: Χιλιάδες νεκρά ψάρια, σμήνη σκουληκιών και μια δυσωδία που παραμένει για μέρες έχουν μετατρέψει τη λίμνη Doddagubbi στη Βεγγαλούρου σε μια έντονη υπενθύμιση των κινδύνων που ενέχουν οι μολυσμένες απορροές για τα αστικά υδατικά συστήματα. Σχεδόν μια εβδομάδα μετά τη μαζική θανάτωση των ψαριών, η λίμνη των 125 στρεμμάτων στην εκλογική περιφέρεια Mahadevapura της Bengaluru παραμένει στο επίκεντρο μιας διαμάχης για…
items.descriptionOriginal: Thousands of dead fish, swarms of maggots and a stench that has lingered for days have turned Doddagubbi Lake in Bengaluru into a stark reminder of the risks polluted runoff poses to urban water bodies. Nearly a week after the mass fish kill, the 125-acre lake in Bengaluru's Mahadevapura Assembly constituency remains at the centre of a dispute over responsibility for the deaths and the delay in removing the carcasses. Villagers allege that neither the Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) nor the Minor Irrigation Department has taken responsibility for addressing the situation. Meanwhile, the Karnataka State Pollution Control Board (KSPCB) has said it will issue notices to Bengaluru Solid Waste Management Limited (BSWML), as leachate from a nearby dumping yard is suspected of contributing to the contamination. The incident raises a larger question for a city whose lakes face mounting pressure from expanding settlements, waste disposal and drainage networks: what happens when rainwater carries pollution into a lake, and the damage goes unaddressed? Thousands of fish, one suspected cause The first explanation for the deaths points to a problem beneath the water's surface. B Chikkanna, deputy director of the Fisheries Department in Mahadevapura ward, told Hindustan Times on Sunday that the initial assessment indicated the fish had died from asphyxiation caused by low levels of dissolved oxygen in the lake. "Prima facie, the fishes died due to asphyxiation. Due to the rains, a large quantity of rainwater mixed with polluted water from Mittaganahalli GBA dumping yard entered Doddagubbi Lake, causing a shortage of oxygen," Chikkanna told the newspaper. The Fisheries Department has begun an inquiry and collected water samples to investigate the deaths. The results will be crucial in establishing the precise cause and identifying the source of contamination. As BSWML and Minor Irrigation Department fail to clear dead fish, Doddagubbi lake is now infested with Maggots. @NewIndianXpress,@XpressBengaluru,@ramupatil_TNIE,@mg_chetan,@aknisreekarthik,@krishnabgowda,@DKShivakumar,@RLR_BTM https://t.co/F32LNINQ33 — Yacoob (@yacoobExpress) October 9, 2026 The suspected sequence of events points to a familiar urban environmental problem. Rainwater that should replenish a lake can also carry pollutants from surrounding land, waste facilities and drainage channels. When this runoff contains high levels of organic waste, the resulting decomposition can reduce the oxygen available to aquatic life. While oxygen depletion is the Fisheries Department's preliminary explanation, investigators must establish what caused oxygen levels to fall and how the pollutants entered the lake. Why oxygen matters to a lake Dissolved oxygen is the oxygen present in water that fish and other aquatic organisms need to survive. When levels drop sharply, fish may be unable to obtain enough oxygen, leading to mass deaths. Research on Bengaluru's lakes has documented similar incidents. In a 2016 report titled Recurring Fish Mortality Episodes in Bangalore Lakes: Sign of Irresponsible and Fragmented Governance , researchers T V Ramachandra, Sincy Varghese, Asulabha K S and Sudarshan Bhat of the Indian Institute of Science's Energy and Wetlands Research Group examined fish deaths in Ulsoor and Devarabisanahalli lakes. Their analysis of water and fish samples linked the deaths to asphyxiation following a sudden decline in dissolved oxygen, associated with the sustained inflow of untreated sewage. Sewage increases the organic load in a water body. As microorganisms break down this material, they consume oxygen, potentially leaving too little for fish and other aquatic organisms. Higher temperatures can intensify these biological processes. The findings offer scientific context for understanding the suspected oxygen depletion at Doddagubbi, although the lake's own test results are needed to establish whether the same mechanism was at work. A study of Bellandur Lake, published in the Journal of Environmental Biology in July 2003, also documented the effects of urban pollution. Researchers J S Chandrashekar, K Lenin Babu and R K Somashekar of Bangalore University's Department of Environmental Sciences reported high biochemical oxygen demand — a measure of the oxygen microorganisms need to break down organic matter — and warned that continued pollution could leave the lake ecologically inactive. Together, these studies show why identifying the source of pollution matters as much as responding to visible fish deaths. A lake's ability to support aquatic life can be compromised long before a mass fish kill makes the damage apparent. When a dumping yard meets a lake Leachate is the contaminated liquid formed when water passes through waste, picking up dissolved and suspended substances. Depending on the type of waste and conditions at the site, it can contain organic pollutants, salts, metals and other potentially harmful compounds. If leachate escapes into nearby drains, ponds or lakes, it can affect water quality and aquatic ecosystems. A study published in the International Journal of Geo-Engineering on 12 December 2018 examined the potential effects of leachate leakage from the Mavallipura municipal solid waste landfill near Bengaluru. Researchers B P Naveen, J Sumalatha and R K Malik investigated the landfill's leachate and surrounding water bodies. Their work documented concerns about runoff entering nearby ponds and open wells and assessed how contaminants could move through soil and spread into surrounding water resources. The research highlights why landfill drainage and leachate containment are particularly important during periods of rainfall. However, it does not establish that the same process caused the fish deaths at Doddagubbi. That question must be answered through local water sampling and an investigation of the drainage pathways. The damage does not end with the fish With dead fish reportedly left uncollected for days, decomposition has produced a foul odour and attracted maggots. What began as a suspected water-quality emergency has become a sanitation concern for nearby communities. If leachate escapes into nearby drains, ponds or lakes, it can affect water quality and aquatic ecosystems. Photograph: (The Hindu) The consequences of leaving the carcasses in place extend beyond the smell. Decomposing organic matter can increase the oxygen demand in the water, while the continued presence of dead fish can complicate efforts to restore the affected area. The extent of any additional deterioration in Doddagubbi Lake's water quality has not yet been established. Investigators must determine the source of contamination, but the immediate response need not wait for every question to be settled. The carcasses need to be removed and disposed of safely, the water needs to be tested, and the route through which pollutants may have entered the lake needs to be identified. What happens after the carcasses are cleared? Removing the dead fish would address the most immediate and visible problem. It would not, by itself, prevent another fish kill. That requires identifying and stopping the source of pollution, assessing the lake's water quality and monitoring dissolved oxygen levels. Authorities must also examine the drains that carry rainwater into the lake, check whether polluted runoff is entering through them, and ensure that nearby waste facilities contain and manage leachate effectively. Research into fish deaths at Ulsoor and Devarabisanahalli lakes in 2016, along with the 2003 study of Bellandur Lake, highlights the consequences of sustained pollution and inadequate management of urban water bodies. The ongoing investigation will determine whether a similar chain of events unfolded at Doddagubbi. Until the sampling results establish the cause, the suspected link to the nearby dumping yard remains an allegation that needs to be investigated. Doddagubbi's case highlights the need to look beyond the immediate crisis. Clearing the carcasses is essential, but protecting the lake in the long term will depend on identifying the source of contamination, preventing further pollution and ensuring that the agencies responsible take action. The fish deaths have made the damage visible. The challenge now is to address the underlying problem before another incident occurs. Sources: ' Mass fish kill leaves Doddagubbi Lake full of maggots' : By Mohammed Yacoob, Published on 9 October 2026 ' Thousands of fish die in Doddagubbi lake' :By Coovercolly Indresh, Published on 5 October 2026 'Recurring Fish Mortality Episodes in Bangalore Lakes: Sign of Irresponsible and Fragmented Governance' : By Energy and Wetlands Research Group, Centre for Ecological Sciences [CES], Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore, Published in 2016

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Soil, Seeds, and Student Power: How Four Canadian Schools are Tackling Food Sovereignty Reading Time: 3 minutes Four schools across Canada show what happens when students are given the tools and trust to build a greenhouse. If you didn’t know it already, students are extremely capable humans, able to tackle projects with a sense of audacity and creativity that (maybe) goes untapped in some older folks. So, when you give them the challenge of growing their own food, they commit, rather wholeheartedly, we should add. It starts as a project, like a club idea, a class assignment, or a response to a funding opportunity, and it becomes something a bit harder to name. A sense of ownership. A connection to where food actually comes from. A reason to show up after school and get dirt under their fingernails. Across four very different Canadian communities, that shift is happening in greenhouses and vertical farms that students built, maintain, and call their own. The Earthlings Climate Club at Sussex Middle School didn’t start big. Five students shared a frustration: nobody at their school was really talking about climate change, so they came up with the idea of building a greenhouse for their breakfast club. The club grew as more students joined, not always because of climate passion, but because their friends were there and it was fun. Those students became advocates too. That’s the lesson the Earthlings want other schools to know: not everyone arrives through the front door of environmental concern, and that’s fine. While waiting for greenhouse materials to arrive (a familiar patience test for rural schools), the students launched a composting program to keep momentum going, earning them a feature in the Telegraph Journal . The greenhouse eventually came together, growing produce for a breakfast club that many students depend on, with ambitions to expand into the cafeteria and local food banks. “Physical hands-on is definitely what I learn through mostly,” said student lead Lyla, “and I feel like we should do more hands-on because it’s way easier to learn.” This next project was never just about the vegetables. For the Ahtahkakoop Cree Nation in Saskatchewan , the greenhouse is one piece of a longer project to rebuild food sovereignty—a way of life that sustained communities for generations before it was systematically disrupted. Youth project lead Jana Sasakamoose framed it quite bluntly: “Many members only get $300 a month to survive off of… It’s hard to meet those needs, let alone basic needs such as food.” Alert Bay students at work building their outdoor greenhouse with the help of First Nations community partners. Photo courtesy of N:OW for Net-Zero . The response was a greenhouse dome chosen for its ability to maximize natural light and air circulation, selected after community consultations on preferred features and plant varieties. Over 250 community members were engaged through canning workshops, gardening sessions, and planning conversations. This is a multi-phase project, with solar panels, underground food storage, and ongoing education all in the pipeline. Alert Bay sits on a small island off the coast of British Columbia, accessible only by ferry. Everything comes by boat, including all the school’s food. With 34 students, 98% of whom are First Nations, and relentlessly windy, rainy weather, a conventional outdoor garden was never going to work. What the school had, though, was community knowledge. Indigenous nations on the island, including the Kwakwaka’wakw, ‘Namgis, and Nawalakw, had already been greenhouse farming, and students came to school with that experience from home. Rather than starting from scratch, Alert Bay Elementary asked its First Nations partners for guidance on suppliers, building techniques, and growing approaches suited to the island’s conditions. The result is a student-maintained greenhouse feeding the school’s hot lunch program, built on the principle of learning from what’s already working. “If we start now,” said student lead Evan, “we can make a difference in the way our school and community think about food and waste.” Oilfields High School in Diamond Valley, Alberta, has been running a vertical farm out of a modified shipping container for years, growing microgreens, lettuce, and herbs that students sell to local grocers, restaurants, and their own school concession. The problem was pests. Before the N:OW for Net-Zero funded biosecurity headerhouse was built, the farm lost 30% of its crops to contamination. Since construction (done by hand with shop students and retired local tradespeople), that loss rate has hit zero. Students at Oilfields High School surround the adult lead, Cindy Watts, as they prep to sell their school-grown microgreens to their student body at lunch. Photo courtesy of N:OW for Net-Zero . CTV News Calgary and CBC have covered the farm , and in April 2026, their Member of Parliament, John Barlow, visited to recognize the students’ work firsthand. This year, the farm launched microgreen smoothies at the school concession twice a week, earned a local grocer’s support for purchasing the school’s greens, and is now actively recruiting youth volunteers and exploring university and company sponsorships to support students as they transition out of high school. A greenhouse, a dome, a modified shipping container, and a grow light in a boot room. The form changes, but the impulse is the same: students decide that food sovereignty isn’t someone else’s problem to solve, and they get to work. The post Soil, Seeds, and Student Power: How Four Canadian Schools are Tackling Food Sovereignty appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.title: Τι με δίδαξε η άνοια για το να ζω μέσα σε μια βαρετή εποχή
items.titleOriginal: What Dementia Taught Me About Living Through a Callous Time
items.description: Την ώρα που ο πρόεδρος Τζο Μπάιντεν έδειχνε τόσο εμφανή σημάδια γνωστικής παρακμής που αναγκάστηκε να εγκαταλείψει την προεδρική κούρσα το 2024, η άνοια του πατέρα μου χειροτέρευε. Έζησε μαζί μας και όμως έζησε σε μια άλλη πραγματικότητα εντελώς. Ένα που δεν καταλάβαινε πια ότι το φαγητό στο πιάτο του ήταν δικό του και το φαγητό της κόρης μου…
items.descriptionOriginal: J ust as President Joe Biden was showing signs of cognitive decline so conspicuous that he was compelled to drop out of the presidential race in 2024, my own father’s dementia was worsening. He lived with us, and yet he lived in another reality entirely. One where he no longer understood that the food on his plate was his, and the food on my daughter’s was hers. One where he grew agitated when we wouldn’t let him walk in a rainstorm. One where he no longer knew my name. Being in the bizarre world of his deteriorating mind was not unlike reading the headlines each day as the months, and then years, went on. My once sweet and Buddhist dad’s abandonment of norms, his misplaced anger, his seemingly selfish relentlessness, were a product of his disease — the nerve cells in his brain were no longer communicating properly. His context for just about everything fell away. Courtney and her father at Thanksgiving. Credit: John Cary The country’s deterioration was different, a deliberate poisoning more than an organic disease, but the parallels were there. It felt pathological how callous and hard our country had become. But there was also something happening underneath my dad’s deterioration. My whole family was learning to collectively care for him — taking him on drives and scream-singing Tom Petty when he would get sundowners (a medical term for late-day confusion in dementia patients), reading Pema Chödrön aloud to him in the backyard, letting him have our ice cream cones when he would reach for them. And our neighbors were in on the tenderness. They’d call when he wandered too far or help him back home when they found him sitting in their unlocked cars. In our local park, when my dad started helping himself to a plate of sandwiches meticulously arranged on a picnic table, the Japanese family they belonged to welcomed this unkempt, white, six-foot-two stranger to their outing as if he were a long lost relative. Likewise, there has been something happening underneath the deterioration of our country. While the headlines reveal the truth of the matter — data centers bulldozing their way into rural communities, masked federal agents yanking delivery workers off their bikes, industry lobbyists buying legislation that allows them to poison our water and air — there are also young people planting community gardens to tackle gun violence in Milwaukee, Wisconsin; caregivers riding their kids to school in bike buses in Montclair, New Jersey; and folks of all ages gathering for the Black Joy Parade in Oakland, California. While some national figures are trying to flood the zone with so much chaos that we can’t keep up, other Americans are working hard to bring running water and indoor plumbing to those who still don’t have it. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] We’re witnessing a reweaving of local fabric, and a renewed curiosity in one another. Parents watching the resurgence of blatant misogyny are intentionally raising boys who embrace their tender feelings and connections. Famously red Texas has had more data center protests than any other state , so perhaps there is more possibility for labor and climate collaboration than we have understood. Leaders in a wide range of faiths weathered the bitter cold of Minneapolis to join local solidarity protests against ICE raids after the tragic death of Renée Good. It seems we are curious again about what role faith might play in our ethical lives together, how we can build a culture of mutual aid in our very unequal communities, and even how we might better understand the economic pain of those who have been abandoned and stereotyped by mainstream media and the political elite. If the last decade or two has been about expanding our horizons, it feels like this one is becoming about humbly narrowing the aperture on our lives and trying to get right with our neighbors, housed and unhoused alike. At a time when A.I. threatens to unravel us in so many ways, economist E.F. Schumacher’s wisdom from his 1973 book Small Is Beautiful: Economics as if People Mattered feels worth reviving: “I have no doubt that it is possible to give a new direction to technological development, a direction that shall lead it back to the real needs of man, and that also means: To the actual size of man. Man is small, and, therefore, small is beautiful.” In the end, this is what saved my family as we took care of my dad; the small moments in the midst of the chaos where we could register his essence intact, where we could devote ourselves to the sacred practice of showing up for him even when it was hard, when we could rest in the awe of it all. It didn’t cure his illness, but it reminded us of us — the fabric, the tenderness, the main thing. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime I wish that same reminder for our country in the months and years ahead — a way to keep our eye on the systemic harm, while keeping our hands in the dirt of our own communities. There are people in our midst who have lost their way through deep delusion, but there are also better angels: The family that offers a strange old man a sandwich; the organizers fighting for clean water for everyone, no exceptions; the daughters of the revolution baking casseroles for the undocumented families hiding in an attic room of their Minneapolis neighbors’ homes. May we never turn away from the systemic injustice, but may we also turn towards the small and beautiful. It’s all real and deeply interconnected, and deserves our fierce attention. The post What Dementia Taught Me About Living Through a Callous Time appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: I f you’re anything like us, you’re not exactly in a congenial mood right now. With the U.S. midterm elections fewer than three weeks away, you might be feeling combat-ready. And who could blame you? Seemingly on the ballot: the very future of the republic, steered by leaders who will shape policy about the climate, A.I., immigration, affordability, wars and many other critical issues. There’s a lot at stake. And yet, for many of us, the way we feel goes beyond those stakes. One part of our brain chugs along analytically, taking stances on legislation, policy and governance. Meanwhile, another part seethes with contempt for those who disagree: They must be stupid, immoral, blind to the facts. Multiply by 340 million, and election season becomes a volatile brew. But there’s hope. While social media algorithms, elected officials, and yes, even our own friends and colleagues, encourage us to close ranks and shut out dissenting voices, others are working in the other direction: reaching out, listening deeply, locating points of connection where they exist, and turning toward those they disagree with, rather than away. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] From now through Election Day, these are the people we’ll journey with. We’ll meet liberals and conservatives who are joining forces despite their differences to oppose data centers and border walls. We’ll talk to students who are turning their college campuses into spaces that welcome an array of opinions, and others participating in cultural exchanges far from their hometowns and comfort zones. We’ll listen in on conversations between “deep canvassers” and the voters they’re hearing out. And we’ll learn how polarization takes hold of the brain — and how, little by little, we can loosen its grip. The Depolarization Project isn’t a call to meet in the middle — it’s an experiment in curiosity. What forces fuel our sense of tribalism? Why do opposing perspectives register as a threat? Can we be open to differences of opinion without compromising our values? Is there hope for those of us who harbor a secret desire to bridge the divides? We know many of you may be skeptical. We hope you’ll take this journey with us regardless, and learn whether we can we fight for what we believe in without closing our minds and our hearts. Illustration by MUTI The post Welcome to the Depolarization Project appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Scientists Develop a Seaweed Coating to Extend the Freshness of Fruit Reading Time: 3 minutes A new seaweed coating can keep strawberries fresher at room temperature than even a refrigerator, offering a lower-carbon way to fight food waste. A new seaweed coating can keep fresh fruit lasting longer than even a refrigerator can. Researchers at the University of British Columbia (UBC) developed the edible dip. In tests, coated strawberries stayed fresh at room temperature for four days or more. Uncoated strawberries left at room temperature molded within just two days. Even refrigerated, untreated berries started molding by day four regardless. Coated strawberries kept in the fridge lasted a full six days, the longest result recorded in the study. The seaweed coating relies on agar, a substance pulled from red algae. Agar is already a common food additive and a popular vegan substitute for gelatin. On its own, though, agar simply forms a thick, unremarkable gel. Doctoral student Ivy Chiu led the study alongside senior researcher Tianxi Yang at UBC. The two published their findings in the Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry in August 2026. Their team says no one had combined these particular ingredients into a coating like this before. Everything changed once researchers added zinc and tannic acid to the mix. Zinc is an essential nutrient, and tannic acid occurs naturally in grapes and tea. Together with agar, these ingredients self-assembled into tiny, evenly spread microparticles. That self-assembly surprised even the research team studying it. The particles form a thin, clear film that seals in moisture and blocks gas exchange. The coating also carries antibacterial and antioxidant properties that further slow spoilage. A seaweed coating enhanced with zinc and tannic acid self-assembles into a thin, clear film of evenly spread microparticles that seals in moisture, blocks gas exchange, and delivers antibacterial and antioxidant properties that slow food spoilage in ways the research team itself did not anticipate. Photo by Clare Kiernan, courtesy of the University of British Columbia . Researchers describe watching the mixture transform from a cloudy liquid into a uniform layer. The process happens within minutes once all three ingredients combine in solution. Dipped fruit emerges with a coating so thin it dries almost invisible. Cut apple slices treated with the seaweed coating stayed fresh for about 24 hours. Untreated slices, by comparison, began visibly decaying within 12 hours. Coated grapes lasted almost 14 days, a full week longer than untreated fruit. Across all three fruits, the coating roughly doubled shelf life compared to no treatment. Weight loss at the four-day mark dropped from 30% down to 13%. Treated fruit also kept more of its vitamin C and antioxidant content. Safety testing found no signs of toxicity in human intestinal cells. Researchers say the coating is safe to eat and washes off easily. It also preserves the fruit’s normal nutritional value throughout storage. A lifecycle analysis compared the coating’s environmental footprint to standard refrigeration. Emissions from the seaweed coating came in lower than or equal to those from cold storage. Researchers say these modest savings could add up across an entire supply chain. Reducing spoilage matters most in a food system that wastes enormous amounts of produce. Nearly half of all food produced in Canada is lost or wasted every year. That waste costs the Canadian economy an estimated $58 billion annually. Fresh fruits and vegetables are especially prone to this kind of loss. They lose moisture quickly and become vulnerable to mold soon after harvest. Long supply chains that rely heavily on refrigeration add further cost and emissions along the way. Cutting down on refrigeration could also ease strain on energy grids. Maintaining cold temperatures from farm to store demands significant infrastructure and power. A coating like this could reduce that demand at several points along the supply chain. They are also testing the seaweed coating across a wider range of fruits and vegetables. The team describes their invention as a practical strategy for building more resilient produce supply chains. Cutting food waste at this scale could ease pressure on refrigeration-heavy supply chains everywhere. A simple seaweed coating might not replace the fridge completely. But it could give fresh produce a longer, greener path from farm to table. The post Scientists Develop a Seaweed Coating to Extend the Freshness of Fruit appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: A bleached coral, stripped of its color and slowly starving, can come back to life in just seven weeks -- if it is placed in contact with a healthy twin. Researchers at Stanford University recently discovered that when genetically identical coral fragments touch, their tissues fuse into what scientist Danny Collins calls "a nutrient highway," and within as little as 36 hours, life-giving algae begin flowing from the healthy fragment into the dying one. The discovery began with a happy accident: a healthy coral slipped against a bleached one in a tank, and someone was paying close enough attention to notice what happened next. The finding won't save coral reefs overnight -- the technique only works between genetic clones, and the ocean keeps warming, which causes coral to bleach. But the findings do open a door. Collins and his team are now exploring whether the algae themselves can be extracted and introduced to bleached corals at scale, without needing the physical bridge at all. While he is clear-eyed about the limits: the real solution is being able to stop coral bleaching in the first place, the horizons feel brighter: "bleached corals aren't a lost cause," he offers.

items.descriptionOriginal: Ever bought a bunch of fresh basil for your pasta , used a few leaves, and watched the rest wilt in the fridge? What if you could simply step onto your balcony and pick a handful whenever you needed them? You don't need a sprawling garden to grow your own basil. With a small pot, some sunlight, and a little care, you can have this fragrant Italian herb growing right at home. But how do you get your basil plant to grow lush, healthy leaves instead of struggling after a few weeks? Dr Mayur Mandrah, a former army major and gardening content creator , shares what works for his own plant. From getting the soil mix right and knowing when to water to a simple pruning trick that encourages bushier growth, he breaks down six practical tips to help you grow fresh basil on your balcony. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Dr Mayur Mandrah, Ex Army Major (@plantwithmayur) Here are his tips for growing a healthy basil plant. 1. Choose the right pot Basil needs sufficient room to spread as it grows. He grows his plant in a six-inch pot and recommends choosing a container that gives the roots enough space. Make sure that the pot has drainage holes at the bottom to allow excess water to escape. His pot has around four holes, which he finds sufficient for his watering routine. He recommends clay pots where possible, although fibre and plastic pots can also be used. Good drainage is important to prevent water from collecting around the roots. 2. Prepare a suitable soil mix For his basil plant, Dr Mayur uses equal quantities of vermicompost and cocopeat. He mixes half vermicompost with half cocopeat to create a growing medium that retains moisture while supplying nutrients. Vermicompost provides nourishment, while cocopeat helps hold water. This easy mix can be used for container gardening, provided the pot drains well. 3. Adjust watering to the weather Basil needs adequate moisture, but its watering requirements change with the season. During the rainy season, the gardener waters his plant about once a week. When watering, he thoroughly soaks the growing medium. In summer, he says the plant may need water every two to three days. For basil growing in a clay pot, he suggests watering every three to four days. You don't need a sprawling garden to grow your own basil. Photograph: (LoveFood) These intervals are based on his experience. Check the soil regularly and adjust watering according to the weather, pot material, and how quickly the growing medium dries. Avoid keeping the soil waterlogged, as this can damage the roots. 4. Provide three to four hours of sunlight Basil needs adequate light to grow well. Dr Mayur recommends keeping the plant on a balcony where it receives around three to four hours of sunlight daily. Morning sunlight is ideal, followed by shade during the hotter part of the day. If you are growing basil indoors, place it near a kitchen window that receives morning sunlight. He prefers growing his plant on the balcony because he has observed that indoor plants tend to develop smaller leaves. 5. Feed the plant regularly The gardener follows an alternating Sunday routine for fertilisation. On the first Sunday, he sprays the plant with seaweed extract. On the second, he uses magnesium sulphate, also known as Epsom salt. He says this routine helps maintain the plant's green foliage. He also adds a little vermicompost to the soil once a month and mixes it into the growing medium. If you follow this approach, use fertilisers according to their product instructions and avoid excessive application. 6. Prune to encourage bushier growth Regular harvesting can help basil develop a fuller appearance. Dr Mayur recommends pinching or cutting the upper growing tips of the stems when picking leaves. Removing these tips encourages lateral branching, allowing more shoots to develop and making the plant bushier. Basil needs sufficient room to spread as it grows. Photograph: (Better Homes & Gardens) He credits his own plant's numerous branches to his wife's frequent harvesting. By regularly picking the upper growth, you can enjoy fresh leaves while encouraging the plant to produce more branches. With the right pot, suitable soil, adequate sunlight, and regular pruning , basil can survive in a small balcony garden. Follow these simple steps to grow this fragrant herb at home and enjoy fresh leaves whenever you prepare your favourite pasta dishes.

items.descriptionOriginal: A child battling cancer had stopped receiving treatment because his family could no longer afford it. Khushbu Taori Modi was still a medical student when she learnt about him. Along with a friend, she traced the child to his home, brought him back and rallied students and others to arrange funds, blood and platelet donations. The child survived. For Khushbu, the experience revealed something she would encounter again and again: people were willing to help, but those who needed support often struggled to find them. Years later, as a government medical officer in Thane and a volunteer with grassroots groups, she saw the same gap. Organisations struggled for funding and volunteers, while people eager to help often did not know where to begin. Could she bring the two together? In February 2024, after nearly ten years in government service, Khushbu left her secure job to explore that question. She wanted to strengthen organisations already doing good work rather than start another NGO. The idea became SewaConnect, a free platform connecting verified social organisations with volunteers, professionals, donors, CSR partners and each other. It has supported more than 100 organisations, facilitated over 50 NGO collaborations and 50 CSR and community partnerships, mobilised over Rs 1 crore in CSR funding and connected more than 100 volunteers. At 6, she was already stopping people from using tobacco Khushbu, now 40, grew up in a middle-class family in Wardha, Maharashtra. A keen student, she was reading newspapers and following current affairs, history and social issues by the age of six. She was especially troubled by tobacco and addiction. As a child, she sometimes took tobacco packets from people's pockets and threw them away, convinced she was helping them quit. "Looking back, it seems amusing, but perhaps that was the beginning of a lifelong commitment to tobacco and addiction prevention," she tells The Better India . The idea became SewaConnect, a free platform connecting verified social organisations with volunteers, professionals, donors, CSR partners and each other. She had wanted to study law, like her father, a criminal lawyer. Encouraged by her family, she instead joined Indira Gandhi Government Medical College, Nagpur, in 2003. She completed her MBBS in 2009, followed by an MD in community medicine at Topiwala National Medical College and BYL Nair Hospital, Mumbai, in May 2013. Government hospitals showed her how health was connected to poverty, education, livelihoods and social support. 'It was a pattern I kept saying' In August 2014, Khushbu joined Thane Municipal Corporation as a Class I Government Medical Officer. She served as Medical Officer, School Health Officer, City TB Officer and COVID-19 In Charge, working across disease control, administration, training and public health programmes. As City TB Officer, she saw how CSR partnerships could strengthen public healthcare. CSR support helped introduce advanced diagnostic equipment, improving access to faster TB diagnosis and treatment. During the pandemic, she also helped build a bed management system in Thane that received national appreciation. "Government can create impact at scale," she says. "A well-planned policy or programme can benefit thousands, sometimes lakhs, of people, and continue making a difference long after the people who initiated it have moved on." Beyond her job, Khushbu continued volunteering and visiting grassroots organisations, something she had done since college. In places such as Gadchiroli, she came across approaches that could be replicated elsewhere. Abhay Bang, Ashish Chaturvedi, Avinash Chowdhury and the work of Hedgewar Hospital influenced her thinking about systems and collaboration. She repeatedly met groups lacking visibility, volunteers, professional expertise or funding , alongside people who wanted to help but did not know how. "It wasn't one incident," she says. "It was a pattern I kept seeing over the years." Why she walked away from a job she loved Khushbu valued her government role and its responsibilities. Her children had grown up seeing her as an officer, and many questioned her decision to resign without another job. Her husband, Gopesh Modi, and a few close friends supported her. At the same time, she had become deeply interested in solid waste management. She undertook residential training, visited dumping grounds and waste processing facilities, and wanted to work more closely on the problem. Opportunities within her role were limited, prompting her to think about how else she could contribute. "I did not leave because I was unhappy with government service. I left because I wanted to contribute differently," she says. She resigned in February 2024 without a fully formed plan. Before the website, there were conversations Khushbu spent the following months visiting organisations, listening to their teams and learning what they needed. At first, she explored collaborating with existing platforms such as GiveIndia, iVolunteer and ConnectFor. She saw a gap: grassroots organisations and voluntary groups needed ways to find supporters and collaborate with each other. Around November 2024, her team began building SewaConnect through social media, gathering information and developing relationships. The website followed later. "Sewaconnect did not begin with a website. It began with conversations," she says. "We already have thousands of organisations and countless individuals doing incredible work. The challenge isn't always the lack of good work. It is that people usually work in isolation," she says. "Our goal isn't to build our own projects. It is to strengthen existing good work and encourage collaboration rather than duplication." 'The real work lies in understanding people' Organisations, voluntary groups, professionals, CSR teams and community groups can register. Social organisations fill out a form, submit relevant documents and undergo verification. Area coordinators visit them, meet their teams and beneficiaries, and understand their work before they are onboarded. It has supported more than 100 organisations, facilitated over 50 NGO collaborations and 50 CSR and community partnerships. Once approved, organisations can update their profiles, share needs and post events or volunteering opportunities. Individuals register based on their interests and skills. An NGO might need a psychologist, physiotherapist, lawyer, trainer, digital expert or mentor. Another may need visibility or guidance from a group that has solved a similar problem. SewaConnect works to make the appropriate introduction. "The website or portal is simply a tool; the real work lies in understanding people, identifying opportunities for collaboration and helping meaningful connections happen," Khushbu says. The platform has two paid interns, around 15 volunteers and a five-person core team. Snehashri Bande handles technology, Kalpita Rakesh Vazhayil manages operations and community engagement, Palak Jain oversees social media and communications, and Vinay Somani advises the team. Volunteers Durgesh Sharma, Chetan Divekar, Vinod Shah, Jashmin Shah, Anjali Gangal and Prakash Rajan support different parts of the work. 'Collaboration creates far greater impact' Pagaria Welfare Foundation was developing community learning centres but needed a strong curriculum. Seva Sahayog Foundation already had one. SewaConnect brought them together. Seva Sahayog's curriculum was adapted for Pagaria's centres, while Pagaria's toy library initiative reached Seva Sahayog's learning centres. Both could build on existing work rather than start from scratch. CA Vaidhei Pagaria, director of Pagaria Welfare Foundation, says the connections helped the organisation implement one community learning centre, five toy libraries, five brain gym centres, one computer learning centre and three menstrual health and hygiene awareness programmes . "Sewaconnect has affirmed our belief that collaboration creates far greater impact than working alone," she says. Another introduction began with a question about Nirmamala, an 18-year-old neurodivergent and speech-impaired girl who had never attended school. SewaConnect connected her with SwayamSiddha's Chembur centre. She began attending regularly, interacting with others, learning skills and receiving a stipend. "Sometimes, all it takes is one person asking a question and the right network responding," Khushbu says. For Swati Mahendra Mohite, founder of Aai Day Care Sanstha in Pen, Maharashtra, support had been hard to find. "Like many grassroots NGOs, our biggest challenge was raising funds and connecting with the right CSR partners and donors. Since we are based in a rural area, gaining visibility among corporate organisations and philanthropists was not easy," she says. Aai Day Care works with more than 70 children and adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities, offering special education, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, vocational training and residential care. Beyond daily sessions, its team spent hours preparing proposals, approaching companies and finding professionals and resources. "Due to limited funding, we sometimes had to postpone improvements, delay therapy sessions or psychological support, and manage every expense very carefully," Swati explains. Through SewaConnect, Aai Day Care partnered with DHL Logistics on its annual operational support project. Swati says it also helped the team approach CSR partners and present its work more confidently. Around November 2024, her team began building SewaConnect through social media, gathering information and developing relationships. "Beyond financial assistance, the platform gave us confidence that our work is being recognised and appreciated," she says. 'Sharing your time & passion is enough' Simran Sanyal, a regional head with a multinational company, heard about SewaConnect through Khushbu. She was introduced to Vidyadaan Sahayak Mandal and now mentors four children. "SewaConnect understood my interests and connected me with the right organisation," she says. "The introduction, coordination and trust were already in place, so I could focus on building relationships with the children instead of worrying about where or how to begin." Soma Chakrabarty, a managing director who also runs Udhayana Foundation, visited organisations with Khushbu and discovered work she had not previously encountered. Through SewaConnect, she began teaching music at a school for children living on the streets and plans to organise fundraising musical programmes. "Contributing to society doesn't always require a huge commitment of money. Sometimes, sharing your time, skills or passion can make a lasting difference," she says. A platform she hopes will run without her SewaConnect has been self-funded and free from the beginning. It does not receive or route donations: contributions from donors and CSR partners go directly to the organisations receiving support. Khushbu wants the platform to remain a neutral bridge rather than compete for resources or run its own projects. She also encourages organisations to plan beyond their founders through succession planning, knowledge sharing, partnerships and even mergers. "Before beginning something new, we should ask ourselves whether an existing organisation is already doing that work and whether strengthening it might create a greater impact," she says. SewaConnect currently operates in Maharashtra, including Mumbai, Thane, Navi Mumbai, Raigad, Pune, Nashik, Wardha, Yavatmal, Beed and Nanded. Khushbu prioritises on-ground verification before expanding elsewhere. She continues her anti-addiction awareness work, which began in childhood and has reached more than 70,000 children and young people. She also works on waste segregation, home composting, reducing single-use plastics and practical community waste management. Over the next few years, she hopes to strengthen SewaConnect, plan for succession and eventually hand it over. Organisations, voluntary groups, professionals, CSR teams and community groups can register. "I don't dream of building a very large organisation around SewaConnect. If, over time, it turns into a self-sustaining ecosystem that can eventually function independently of me, I would consider that a success," she says. Her understanding of impact has changed since her years in public health. "Earlier I measured impact by the number of patients treated or programmes implemented. Today, I also measure it by the number of meaningful relationships created," she says. Years after finding help for a child whose cancer treatment had stopped, she is working to make such connections easier for others. "India doesn't lack people willing to help, and it certainly doesn't lack people doing good work. What we often lack are trusted connections between the two," Khushbu concludes All pictures courtesy Dr Khushbu Taori Modi.

Το θέμα είναι, όλα αυτά τα απορρίμματα φύλλων, αυτά τα κούφια στελέχη, εκείνα τα μπαλώματα της σκληρής νεκρής φυτικής ύλης; Th…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Every fall there’s a pull to tidy things up. Cut back the perennials, rake the leaves, clear the beds, put the garden to rest. It feels satisfying, honestly, and spring does seem to start from a cleaner place. The thing is, all that leaf litter, those hollow stems, those patches of scraggly dead plant matter? That’s where the bees are. Over 3,600 bee species are native to the United States, and most of them are not honey bees. It’s the native wild bees, including mason bees, leafcutters, mining bees, long-horned bees, bumble bees, and hundreds of others, that are in steep decline. Most are solitary: each female builds her own nest, lays her eggs, stocks them with food, seals them up, and dies. As Matthew Shepherd , Director of Outreach and Education at the Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation , explains, the offspring “complete most of their life stages in the cell, remaining there until the following year, when they emerge at the same season their mother was active.” That nest is almost certainly somewhere in your garden. Sam Droege , Wildlife Biologist at the USGS, says wild bees are nesting above ground and in the ground somewhere nearby no matter where you live. Ecological landscape designer Kim Eierman puts it plainly: “You may have hundreds or even thousands of individual bees using your landscape. The good news is that you don’t have to do much to give them a place to live.” Most of what they need is already there, and the beauty of this solution is that all you have to do is less. What to do with the fallen leaves Move them rather than bag them. Bumble bee queens hibernate by digging a few inches underground or into leaf mulch, so piling leaves onto flower beds or into a back corner of the yard makes them a winter home. Leaf piles also give fireflies and other small garden creatures a place to wait out the cold. Shepherd’s guidance: remove leaves from anywhere they’re a slip hazard or blocking a drain, but keep them on flower borders, along the base of a hedge, or tucked into a back corner. A rake or broom does the job without the disturbance a leaf blower causes. Think twice before cutting everything back Pruning everything to the ground in fall can cost wild bees their winter home. “Avoiding the typical fall cleanup on plants and keeping stems of perennials and annuals creates nesting opportunities for tunnel-nesting bees such as small carpenter bees and leafcutters,” Shepherd says. The birds appreciate it too; they’ll forage on the seedheads through winter. If a tidy front yard matters to you, Droege has a workable compromise: cut back to about a foot tall instead of to the ground. “A plant needs to be damaged or dead for bees to be able to use it,” he says, so a shorter cut still creates usable nesting structure without looking neglected. If you’re already mid-cleanup, don’t compost what you’ve cut. “If any bees are already nesting in the stems, composting them will cause the end of that cycle,” Droege says. A loose pile left on the ground or behind the shed keeps the cycle going. Eierman adds that pithy stems from elderberry, raspberry, hydrangea, and Joe Pye weed are especially useful to cavity-nesting bees and can be bundled and left in place through winter. Leave brush piles, snags, and cane fruit stems Pruned branches can go into a brush pile rather than the compost. Loose piles don’t do much; Eierman notes they need to be “fairly tight and dense, providing cavities that shelter bees from rain.” Dead or dying trees are candidates for keeping if they’re well away from the house. These are called snags. They develop hollow passages over time as beetles tunnel through the dead wood, and cavity-nesting bees use those passages the following season. A snag that’s too tall to feel comfortable about can be cut back to a manageable height without losing what makes it useful. For cane fruits like raspberries, blackberries, and boysenberries, Droege says the same logic applies. “Cane fruits only fruit in year two,” he says. “Instead of cutting them to the ground, trimming them to a foot tall provides the best nesting material for a whole series of native wild bees.” Leave bare patches of soil undisturbed Most native bees nest in the ground and need bare, uncompacted soil to excavate their nests. “Don’t try to repair all the bare ground — leave the open areas, as bees like to nest there,” says Droege. Sandy or loamy soil in a sunny spot is ideal, but even a few square feet counts. If a bare patch feels too sparse, Eierman says planting very sparsely may still leave enough exposed soil between plants; just skip the mulch or landscape fabric, as both block bees from getting in. Treat it as wild habitat rather than an incomplete garden bed: no tilling, no cleaning up, not even in spring. Keep some flowers going through fall Most bees have wrapped up their nesting cycle by the time temperatures drop, but sweat bees and mining bees are still out foraging late in the season. Goldenrod and asters are the flowers they’re looking for. Having something in bloom through fall, and building toward a range of bloom times from spring through the end of the season, gives different species something to work with at different points in the year. “Expanding your garden for next spring and reducing your lawn is the biggest thing you can do for wild bees ,” Droege says. Eierman says it best: “You may have hundreds or even thousands of individual bees using your landscape. The good news is that you don’t have to do much to give them a place to live.” Leave the leaves. Don’t compost the stems. Keep a corner wild. That’s most of it. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post What to leave alone in your garden this October to help overwintering bees first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .
