items.descriptionOriginal: I n his first year at the University of California, Davis, Liam commuted three hours a day from his family’s home in the Bay Area to campus and back again. The round-trip train tickets were expensive, but not as pricey as renting an apartment in the Central Valley college town. Then, partway through the school year, conflict with his family upended Liam’s living arrangement. “I didn’t have anywhere to go,” he says. “It wasn’t like anybody was supporting me, and the money that I did have was very little.” Liam bounced from place to place before landing at Aggie House , where he spent the next nine months living a short distance from campus with roommates who were also struggling to find a place to call home. Aggie House isn’t a typical university dorm or homeless shelter: It’s a collection of low-cost apartments, created and run by UC Davis students, for classmates who are facing housing insecurity. The kitchen at the Y2Y shelter. About 3.5 million people between the ages of 18 and 25 face homelessness each year in the U.S., increasing their vulnerability to harms including trafficking, incarceration and suicide. Photo courtesy of Y2Y As high costs and low vacancies squeeze property markets across the country, housing remedies for college students exist to support young people during a particularly volatile stage of adulthood. Start-ups like Depaul USA and the Neighborhood Coalition For Shelter run initiatives such as the Dax Program and NCS Scholars that provide room, board and mentorship to college students. Yet a crucial, sometimes overlooked dimension of this assistance is the nationwide network of young adults stepping up for each other by establishing and operating housing solutions dedicated to their age group. Some cater specifically to students; others welcome anybody in their late teens to early 20s who needs a place to stay. Bound by a sense of solidarity, these spaces foster a sense of belonging and camaraderie as young people navigate school, careers and the challenges of early adulthood. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] “I think sometimes, in general shelters, it can be harder for people to understand what a student is going through,” says Hayven Angelique Pfister, a fourth-year human biology student at UC Davis and the external co-president of Aggie House. And because all the residents and volunteers there share the experience of being students, she says, “it’s easier [and] more comfortable.” A young person in the U.S. may experience homelessness due to a combination of serious family issues and broader systemic challenges . Common factors include family conflict, abuse or rejection — particularly for LGBTQ+ youth — alongside economic instability, a lack of affordable housing and aging out of public systems like foster care. The upshot is that about 3.5 million people between the ages of 18 and 25 face homelessness each year in the U.S., a situation that makes them particularly vulnerable to harms such as trafficking, violence, extremely poor physical and mental health, incarceration and suicide. Each of Y2Y’s sleeping bunks is equipped with a Plexiglas shutter for privacy, lockable storage, individual lighting and power outlets for recharging electronics. Photo courtesy of Y2Y “Young people experience a lot of trauma before homelessness, and they’re experiencing more trauma while they’re homeless,” says Darla Bardine, executive director of the National Network for Youth, a public education and policy advocacy organization focused on preventing and ending youth homelessness in America. “That’s why our perspective is: The earlier you can identify a young person experiencing homelessness and get them into help, you can hopefully prevent more compounded trauma.” The key to addressing homelessness among those under 25, Bardine says, is partnership with other young people. “They know where young people hang out,” Bardine says. “It’s easier for them to build that trusting relationship with young people because they have lived it.” Students established Aggie House at UC Davis in 2021 as part of a network of shelters on three California campuses that aim to ensure no student is left without a place to live. Many people erroneously assume that people who experience homelessness don’t work, Pfister says. “We have a lot of people who are working, who are getting financial aid,” she says. “They still can’t afford to get housing. They still can’t get what they need.” Aggie House offers accommodations for up to a year, and residents pay rent — usually $200 to $300 monthly, which is 90 percent less than the average cost of rent in Davis. Rent increases by $50 monthly to incentivize people to move on. Guests must be UC Davis students, and are vetted through an application and interview process to determine their need for housing, with many having been referred through a center run by the university that aims to ensure students’ basic needs are met. The shelter is run entirely by undergraduate volunteers on 7 p.m. to 11 p.m shifts, whose role is partly to help build social connections. A few nights a week, the volunteers take turns preparing dinner for residents. One of Pfister’s favorites she made was a sushi bake with layers of salmon, rice and seaweed. Over meals, residents and volunteers chat about pop culture, school, religion and politics. Meanwhile, over in the basement of the white-clapboard First Parish church around the corner from Harvard Square in Cambridge, Massachusetts, 22 bunks are staggered in three tiers, separated by lime green walls and white polka-dotted privacy screens. From October through April, and again for a shorter summer season, Y2Y shelter provides housing for up to 30 days for people between the ages of 18 and 24. Unlike Aggie House, Y2Y doesn’t specifically cater to students; many guests are LGBTQ+ who lost family support, or aged out of foster care. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime Y2Y was founded by two Harvard students in 2015, in part to address safety concerns among youth in adult shelters, according to Caleb Oh, Y2Y’s administrative director who is studying math and statistics at Harvard University. Y2Y offers an alternative for young people who don’t get into nearby all-age emergency shelters, or feel unsafe using them. Young adults facing homelessness often avoid adult shelters and child welfare systems because of fears of exposure to substance use or sexual assault, or because of past negative experiences. “Being unhoused is incredibly frightening, incredibly isolating,” Oh says. He’s been told by people who have stayed at the youth-led shelter that the environment is less stressful than alternatives. “What Y2Y can provide,” he says, “is just being social and having a community.” At weekly youth advisory meetings, guests give feedback on the shelter, catch up and play board games. Student volunteers from universities and neighborhoods across the Boston area serve as case managers, helping guests navigate housing support programs and connecting them with other services so they have a next place to stay. This summer, four guests moved into rental units, five went on to transitional housing and four went to a different shelter with professional case management. Y2Y’s main living space. Many guests at the shelter are LGBTQ+ who lost family support, or aged out of foster care. Photo courtesy of Y2Y “I think what we get right is putting not just our guests first but attempting to let them put themselves first,” Oh says. “We are more facilitators than anything.” One of the biggest challenges for youth-led shelters is capacity. Y2Y only operates through the winter and part of the summer, when students are available to staff the shelter, and there’s a waitlist for openings. Likewise, because the shelters’ volunteers are students, they have limited bandwidth to give while balancing school. Volunteers are also learning as they go, unlike professionally trained staff at other shelters. But that youth-led perspective can also be a significant advantage. Liam says the upperclassman volunteers who supported him had navigated the same systems he then had to face. After he arrived, his student case manager helped him make sense of financial aid, enroll in health insurance, get a job, save up money and eventually find an apartment, which he now shares with roommates. He moved in about a month ago. The post Young Adults Are Building Safe Spaces for Unhoused Peers appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Wildlife Crossings in Florida are Saving Panthers from Highway Deaths Reading Time: 3 minutes Wildlife crossings in Florida are turning deadly highways into safe passageways for one of America’s rarest cats. Wildlife crossings in Florida now exist in dozens of locations across South Florida. These structures let panthers move without crossing traffic. The results are already changing outcomes for a species once pushed to the brink, and the wildlife crossings today serve as a model other states are watching closely. The Florida panther used to roam across the entire Southeast. Today its only breeding population lives in Southwest Florida. That population now survives on less than 5% of its historic habitat. Panthers once shared their range with black bears, red wolves, and other predators across the Southeast. Hunting and land conversion eliminated most of these populations over the past century. Today conservationists work to protect the remaining core habitat in Big Cypress and the greater Everglades ecosystem. Roads make that shrinking habitat even more dangerous. In 2024 alone, drivers struck and killed 30 panthers. Each loss matters for a population this small and fragile, which is why wildlife crossings in Florida have become such an urgent conservation priority. Panthers need large territories to hunt, find mates, and raise young. When roads slice through that territory, populations become isolated. Isolated populations struggle to recover and stay healthy over time. Interstate 75, known locally as Alligator Alley, carries millions of travelers through South Florida every year. It also cuts straight through vital panther habitat. Black bears, deer, bobcats, alligators, and otters share this same landscape. Wildlife crossings in Florida benefit far more than panthers, with bobcats, deer, and black bears all documented using the same underpasses, proving that a single well-placed crossing stretches conservation dollars across an entire ecosystem. Photo courtesy of Florida Wildlife Federation . When builders planned this highway decades ago, they faced a 40-mile stretch of critical panther territory. Rather than leaving a permanent barrier, the Florida Department of Transportation added crossings into the design. That early decision is one of the clearest examples of wildlife crossings in Florida in practice. Completed in the early 1990s, the project included 24 wildlife underpasses and 12 modified bridges. Planners also added continuous fencing along all 40 miles. The fencing steers animals toward safe crossing points instead of open lanes. A Transportation Research Board study later tracked bobcats, deer, and black bears alongside panthers using these underpasses. That data confirmed multiple species benefit from a single, well-placed crossing. Shared infrastructure like this stretches conservation dollars further across the whole ecosystem. State Route 29 tells a similar story. This road splits the Florida Panther National Wildlife Refuge from the Big Cypress Wildlife Management Area. One stretch, called Owl Hammock, ranks among the most dangerous spots for panthers, bears, and drivers alike. Florida’s transportation department is working on a fix there, too. Crews will build a new wildlife bridge over Barron River Canal. They will also raise the road 8 feet, add a culvert underneath, and install 2 miles of new fencing. The Owl Hammock project carries a price tag of $8.67 million. That investment reflects a broader pattern statewide. Florida now has 60 wildlife crossings and bridges in operation. Wildlife bridges like this also protect panther genetic diversity by connecting isolated groups. Without these connections, inbreeding threatens the population’s long-term health. Genetic diversity remains one of the biggest challenges to full panther recovery. Combining crossing structures with fencing has measurably reduced wildlife deaths. Researchers have documented panthers and other animals successfully using these crossings. Well-designed infrastructure can reconnect habitat while keeping both animals and drivers safer, reinforcing why wildlife crossings in Florida matter far beyond one species. Still, panthers keep dying on Florida roads, especially young cats still learning their territory. That reality shows the work is far from finished. More crossings, more fencing, and more funding are needed to keep this progress going. Congress has a chance to build on what Florida has already proven works. Reauthorizing the Wildlife Crossing Pilot Program is the next step that could extend this success well beyond Florida. Florida’s highways show that people and panthers do not have to compete for the same ground. Smart infrastructure lets both share the landscape safely. That balance took decades of planning, and it still needs steady support to last. The panther’s story is far from over. But every underpass, bridge, and stretch of fencing adds another chance for this species to recover. Florida’s roads are proving that wildlife crossings in Florida can go hand in hand with moving people forward. The post How Wildlife Crossings in Florida are Saving Panthers from Highway Deaths appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Leslie Gomez Rivera didn't like anything about the cafeteria at her Brooklyn high school, and had little hope it would change. Then she heard about Youth Food Advocates that supports students to advocate for change. They provided Leslie with the information and tools to do something about it. Leslie created a survey of other students, and collaborated with the cafeteria manager and principal. Her findings helped inspire the school to offer foods students liked to eat, student tasting and approval of new menu items, more efficient and inviting food displays, and comfortable seating. "This was one of the pivotal moments when I realized that if you want it done, you can do it yourself," Rivera said. "I felt like this was something that not only affects my everyday [life], but that the next generation … would be affected. And if I could do something about it, I would."

items.title: Πληρώσαμε φοιτητές περίπου 5 $ τη νύχτα για να κοιμούνται τουλάχιστον 7 ώρες — και οι βαθμοί τους βελτιώθηκαν γρήγορα
items.titleOriginal: We Paid College Students About $5 a Night to Sleep at Least 7 Hours — And Their Grades Quickly Improved
items.description: Αυτό το άρθρο γράφτηκε από τον Osea Giuntella, αναπληρωτή καθηγητή οικονομικών στο Πανεπιστήμιο του Πίτσμπουργκ, τη Sally Sadoff, καθηγήτρια οικονομικών και στρατηγικής στο Πανεπιστήμιο της Καλιφόρνια στο Σαν Ντιέγκο και τη Silvia Saccardo, καθηγήτρια κοινωνικών επιστημών και επιστημών αποφάσεων στο Πανεπιστήμιο Carnegie Mellon, για το The Conversation — μια μη κερδοσκοπική είδηση ​​ή…
items.descriptionOriginal: This article was written by Osea Giuntella , an associate professor of economics at the University of Pittsburgh, Sally Sadoff , a professor of economics and strategy at the University of California, San Diego, and Silvia Saccardo , a professor of social and decision sciences at Carnegie Mellon University, for The Conversation — a nonprofit news organization dedicated to sharing the knowledge of researchers and scientists, under a Creative Commons license . Read the original article here . Paying college students about $5 a night to sleep seven hours got them a quarter more nights of adequate sleep — and better grades. That is what we found in a study we published in July 2026 . We gave more than 1,100 undergraduates at University of Pittsburgh a Fitbit — a wearable activity tracker that looks similar to a watch — and an app that sent bedtime reminders and morning feedback. We randomly chose 468 students and paid them about $5 for every night they slept at least seven hours, over the course of four weeks. We verified how much they slept using the device they wore. The students were about 19 years old, on average, and half of them were first-year students. Roughly 72% of them were women. About 55% were white, 28% Asian, 9% Black, and 4% Hispanic. Our study shows that offering an immediate financial reward can help students meet a seven-hour sleep goal, and that those effects can persist up to a month beyond when the students are paid. Not Just a Student Problem About one-third of American adults sleep less than seven hours a night, and a similar share say they wish they slept more. Among adolescents and young adults, roughly two-thirds routinely fall short of getting seven hours of sleep a night — the amount of shut-eye that health authorities recommend . One prominent sleep researcher has called sleep deprivation the most prevalent high-risk behavior. Short sleep is linked to obesity, diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, stroke, and early death . Irregular sleep predicts mortality risk even more than sleep duration does . Sleep loss shows up in decision-making, even when it comes to issues like whether people vote . Students Are Running on Empty Before we changed anything, the average student in our study slept 6.6 hours a night . Half were going to bed after 1 a.m. on average — a quarter after 2 a.m. Students got the recommended seven hours of sleep on a typical weeknight on only 43% of their nights, and more than 85% fell short at least once a week. They also did not know how much sleep they were getting. Two-thirds told us they usually slept seven hours — the trackers showed only about one-third of students slept that much on even three nights out of five. And 94% said their ideal night of sleep was longer than the one they were getting. What the Money Bought The 468 students we offered nightly payments reached seven hours of sleep on 26% more nights than 380 students who were not offered the money. That is a large shift for a group in which fewer than half were hitting the mark to begin with. Students receiving the monetary incentive slept 19 more minutes per school night, roughly the difference between closing the laptop at 11:40 p.m. or at midnight. Among students receiving the payment incentive, their GPA rose by about 0.08 points that semester — roughly a quarter of the gap between students who arrived with above-average and below-average high school grades. Once the payments stopped after four weeks, students who had received the money were still sleeping about eight minutes longer per night for the remaining three to four weeks of the study. The effect was smaller than during our study, but our findings suggest that some of the change in sleep habits persisted for up to a month after the end of the incentive. The effects of the intervention on sleep and GPA were largest among first-term freshmen, whose routines are not yet necessarily fixed. Glow Images/Getty Images Universities spend heavily on helping students learn. Very few treat sleep as part of that investment. Rewards Work — if They Come Right Away Timing mattered too: Delivering the payment as a lump sum at the end of the semester, rather than every morning, produced only about two-thirds of the effect on sleep. The effects of the intervention on GPA faded over a couple of academic terms. Grades remained higher in the following semester, but two semesters later we could no longer detect an effect. Bedtime reminders and morning feedback on their own — with no money attached — had little effect. Students who received them slept only marginally more. The problem was not motivation: Nearly all said they wanted more sleep than they were getting. The challenge was following through on that intention night after night. Investing in Sleep Our results show that universities should look at how the environment they create fosters or discourages good sleep habits. Late evening deadlines to submit assignments and early classes can both make it harder for students to get enough sleep. Changing some of these features costs little compared with many academic support programs, and it may be worth testing alongside other interventions aimed directly at students. Reminders and feedback might also work better if they change over time, rather than becoming familiar and easy to tune out. Very few universities or students treat sleep as part of an investment in education, or ask whether the schedules and incentives schools create make adequate sleep harder. Our results suggest they should. RELATED: The 5 Sleep Languages: How Knowing Yours Could Help You Get Better Rest

items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Υπάρχει ένα συγκεκριμένο είδος βραδινής σπείρας της Κυριακής που συμβαίνει όταν έχετε αφιερώσει είκοσι λεπτά διαβάζοντας για ένα συστατικό που δεν έχετε ακούσει ποτέ και είστε πλέον πεπεισμένοι ότι ολόκληρη η ρουτίνα σας είναι λάθος. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM There’s a particular kind of Sunday evening spiral that happens when you’ve spent twenty minutes reading about an ingredient you’ve never heard of, and you’re now convinced your entire routine is wrong. Skin care has never been better at making us feel behind. Five board-certified dermatologists, when asked which habits they most wish patients would break, kept arriving at the same place: most of us are doing too much, not too little. Some of what follows, you’ve heard before. Some of it will stick in a way the usual advice doesn’t. Stop chasing skin care trends “Skin care is a long game,” says Dr. Laurel Naversen Geraghty , a board-certified dermatologist in Medford, Oregon. “It’s not how much you blast your face with new ingredients; it’s the good, proven steps that you stick to over time.” That runs counter to how skin care gets marketed, where the week’s buzzy ingredient has a way of making whatever you already own feel outdated. Dr. Ava Shamban , a board-certified dermatologist in Los Angeles, keeps seeing young patients come in with reactive, inflamed skin from doing too much at once. “I’ll ask, ‘Okay, three weeks ago, what were you doing?'” The answer is almost always a new stack of products. The risk isn’t just wasted money. Layering too many active ingredients can compromise the skin barrier, leading to bumps, flakes, itchy rashes, and sensitivity that can “take time, a dermatologist consultation, and medication to calm and reverse,” Dr. Geraghty says. Her rule: don’t introduce more than one new product or ingredient at a time, and give anything at least three months before deciding it isn’t working. “Don’t give up on a proven ingredient after a few days or a week.” With retinoids, meaningful results take around six months. With peptides, two to three months. Trends come and go, but as Dr. Geraghty puts it, “your skin has to last you a lifetime.” Build sunscreen into an existing habit Sun exposure is the leading cause of skin aging and the leading cause of skin cancer. “UV light raises the risk for cancer, just like smoking and asbestos raise the risk of cancer,” says Dr. Geraghty. Every dermatologist in this article made some version of that point, with varying degrees of exasperation. Most people know they should wear sunscreen . Most people don’t do it every day. Dr. Corey Hartman , a board-certified dermatologist in Birmingham, Alabama, has a fix: put sunscreen right next to your toothbrush. “It’s something you do every single day after brushing your teeth. That way you don’t have to wonder and guess if you put it on.” Build it into a routine you’re already doing, and it becomes automatic. Aim for SPF 35 or higher and hit the areas people routinely miss: the sides of the nose, the temples, the ears, and above the upper lip. The one-squeeze rule for pimple popping This might be the hardest habit on this list. Dr. Hartman is candid: “I’m guilty of it myself.” His answer isn’t to quit entirely. It’s a limit. “You get one good squeeze,” he says. If the pimple is ready, it comes out. If it doesn’t come out on the first try, stop. Continuing only pushes bacteria deeper, delays healing, and raises the chances of post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, the dark spots that can stick around long after the pimple itself is gone. After a successful squeeze, cover the spot with a hydrocolloid pimple patch. If nothing happened, use a salicylic acid spot treatment instead. Covering it either way makes the next step easier: it’s hard to keep picking at something that’s already covered. One gentle cleanser is almost always enough More cleanser doesn’t mean cleaner skin. “People get very exuberant with their cleansing technique,” says Dr. Hartman. Washcloths, silicone brushes, and mesh sponges are all too aggressive and prone to causing redness, irritation, and dryness. Double-cleansing, using two face washes in sequence, works well for people who wear heavy makeup or have very oily skin. Most people are neither. “I just think more people are double-cleansing than really need to be, and they end up over-cleansing,” Dr. Hartman says. One gentle, fragrance-free cleanser is usually all it takes. Wash your face when you get home, not right before bed If nighttime face washing keeps getting skipped because you’re exhausted, Dr. Rachel Nazarian , a board-certified dermatologist in New York City, has a practical fix: stop treating it as a bedtime task. “Rather than waiting until bedtime, shift it earlier—when you get home, change your clothes, wash your face, remove your makeup.” Do it when you still have energy, and the habit holds. Cleansing wipes aren’t a substitute. They feel like they’re doing something, but they leave behind residue that can irritate and dry out skin, and they don’t remove the dirt, bacteria, and makeup that built up during the day. You need soap and water. Stop scratching your scalp This is the one that tends to catch people off guard. Scratching an itchy scalp, even casually a couple of times a day, can cause hair breakage, according to a 2024 study in the Archives of Dermatological Research , and over time can contribute to thinning. Dr. Jeanine Downie , a board-certified dermatologist in Montclair, New Jersey, is blunt: “Then you’re adding the tension of scratching? Seriously?” The timeline is shorter than you’d think. Regular scratching can cause breakage in less than a week, and recovery takes two to three months of keeping your hands off. If your scalp is itchy, address the itch rather than scratch it. An anti-inflammatory shampoo is a reasonable first move for common culprits like dandruff or mild psoriasis . For itch without an obvious cause, a dermatologist can figure out what’s driving it and treat it at the source. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post The common skin care mistakes dermatologists say are working against your routine first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.titleOriginal: How a floating shade can help coral survive a marine heatwave
items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST DAILY Όταν οι δύτες εγκατέστησαν αιωρούμενες δομές σκιάς πάνω από 20 αποικίες κοραλλιών του εγκεφάλου στο κάτω μέρος της Florida Keys τον Αύγουστο του 2024, τα κοράλλια από κάτω άρχισαν να ανακτούν το χρώμα τους. Οι 20 αποικίες που έμειναν απροστάτευτες έγιναν πιο ωχρές κατά τη διάρκεια της πιο καυτής περιόδου της σεζόν. Αυτό ήταν κατά τη διάρκεια του δεύτερου υψηλότερου θερμικού στρες του 2024…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM When divers installed floating shade structures over 20 colonies of brain coral in the lower Florida Keys in August 2024, the corals underneath began recovering their color. The 20 colonies left unprotected grew paler through the hottest stretch of the season. That was during 2024’s second-highest heat stress year on record at the site since 1985. The results appear in Frontiers in Marine Science . The shades were made from PVC frames and nylon mesh, suspended roughly 12 inches (30 centimeters) above the coral. They weren’t cooling the water. They were blocking the intense sunlight and ultraviolet radiation that amplifies heat-related bleaching. Why Florida’s 2023 heatwave made this study necessary In the summer of 2023, a record marine heatwave hit the Florida Keys. At most monitored sites, every kind of coral bleached. Branching corals, including the staghorn and elkhorn species, were nearly wiped out. At one inshore location, more than half of the corals researchers were tracking lost some or all their living tissue. Karen Neely of Nova Southeastern University, the study’s lead author, described the umbrella project as a direct response. “This study stemmed directly from that event: we wanted to provide proof of concept for tools to save targeted corals in similar future events,” she said. “ Heat-related coral bleaching is probably the biggest threat to reefs worldwide. Solutions like shading can offer temporary protection on small scales.” The scale of the global bleaching crisis Scale is where the Florida experiment runs into its limits. On August 22, the average global sea surface temperature outside the polar regions hit 21.1 degrees Celsius (70 degrees Fahrenheit), the highest daily reading on record. Between 2023 and 2024, global hard coral cover fell by 8.9 percent, the largest single-year decline ever measured. By March 2025, 84 percent of the world’s reefs had experienced temperatures high enough to cause bleaching, and parts of Australia’s Great Barrier Reef had just recorded their worst annual losses of living coral in nearly 40 years of monitoring. Bleaching events are also arriving more frequently. The Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network reported in August that they now occur roughly every five to six years, compared with about once a decade in the past. Corals can recover between events if temperatures drop in time. The problem is that time is getting shorter. The limits of shading as a strategy The researchers are direct about what these results don’t mean. Covering entire reefs with shade structures isn’t practical, and the study monitored individual colonies rather than reef systems. “Scaling is the big limitation of this study,” Neely said. “Shading is not a cure-all.” What the intervention does is buy time. During extreme heat events , targeted shading can protect specific corals, species that take decades to grow back and anchor the ecosystems around them. But reef survival at any meaningful scale requires slowing ocean warming, and that means emissions reductions well beyond what shade structures can address. Coral reefs cover less than 0.2 percent of the ocean floor but shelter at least a quarter of all marine species and buffer coastlines from erosion and storm surge. The Florida study is useful for protecting the most important specimens while a crisis is happening. It doesn’t change the frequency at which those crises arrive. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post How a floating shade can help coral survive a marine heatwave first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

Ο 32χρονος φωτογράφος με έδρα το Τόκιο, έχει εξερευνήσει 36 χώρες, τραβώντας συναρπαστικές φωτογραφίες από μέρη που δεν απεικονίζονται - τα σημεία που αγαπά που συνήθως δεν μπαίνουν στους τουριστικούς οδηγούς. Το ενδιαφέρον του…
items.descriptionOriginal: When you picture Nevada in your mind, you likely conjure the bright lights of the Las Vegas Strip. Kohki Yamaguchi thinks of starry skies and donkeys. The Tokyo-based photographer, 32, has explored 36 countries, snapping breathtaking photos of unpictured places — the spots he loves that don’t typically make it into the tourist guides. His interest in photography first piqued 10 years ago when he finished university and started taking photos of abandoned buildings. His philosophy around his craft includes noticing “what others might overlook,” his webs ite states, which ties into his travel work. In 2023, Yamaguchi decided to visit Iraq to take street photographs of people talking to each other and recalled he could “feel the humanity very strongly,” per SWNS. Kohki Yamaguchi / SWNS Kohki Yamaguchi / SWNS Other destinations he’s captured include the Chinese countryside and the aforementioned Nevada. “Me and a friend went there just because you can see the stars clearly at night,” he told the outlet. “But surprisingly, more than the stars, we found these random roads had donkeys walking about.” Yamaguchi said he recently looked at a graph of the world’s most-photographed areas and was shocked to see the places he’s loved didn’t make it on the list. “Those places are not just the least photographed but also just people don’t really consider that as an ideal bucket list destination,” he noted. Kohki Yamaguchi / SWNS Kohki Yamaguchi / SWNS Today, his photography has earned him 1.3 million followers on Instagram alone , and he said he’s grateful when people feel inspired to take their own photos after seeing his work. “I truly believe photography can enhance the way we see things and remember them,” Yamaguchi said. “I’m very happy if someone can start photography even if it’s just as a hobby.” And for all of the traveling he’s done, he most appreciates showing people the special, unpictured places in his native Japan: “Traveling to other countries and comparing them to my own country I realized — I’m not sure how to put it into one word to describe it — but how lucky I am to be from this country.” Indeed, his favorite photo he’s ever taken is of a whimsical curb in Tokyo that’s painted to resemble a piece of tamago sushi, a sweet Japanese omelet held in place atop rice with a strip of nori. “It’s something you have to be observant to spot,” Yamaguchi said. Kohki Yamaguchi / SWNS Kohki Yamaguchi / SWNS Here are the countries he’s visited so far: Japan U.S. Australia New Zealand Taiwan Hong Kong China Macau Thailand Singapore Indonesia Malaysia Fiji England France Poland Italy Monaco Germany Austria Netherlands Switzerland Czech Republic Belgium Turkey Greece Peru Russia (Sakhalin Island) UAE Qatar Sweden Finland Iceland South Africa Iraq Norway This article was originally written by Emily Phillips for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Sustainable Fleet Vehicle Maintenance Tips for the Cold Months Ahead Reading Time: 6 minutes Sustainable Fleet Vehicle Maintenance Tips for the Cold Months One vehicle that will not start on a January morning is an inconvenience. Five of them, on the same morning, with crews waiting and jobs booked, is a lost day of revenue. Winter does not usually create new problems in a fleet so much as expose the ones that were already there: a battery near the end of its life, tires that were fine in summer, diesel that was never treated for the cold. Fleets that get through winter smoothly tend to start preparing in the fall. This guide covers: Tires and wheels that suit a working fleet in winter Scheduling preventive maintenance before the first freeze Diesel fuel gelling and diesel exhaust fluid in the cold Driver checks and emergency kits for every vehicle At a Glance Takeaway Detail Start in the fall Battery tests, tire changeovers and fuel treatment are easier to schedule before the first cold snap. Check pressure after temperature swings Tire pressure drops as it gets colder, so pre-trip checks should include a gauge, not just a glance. Steel wheels suit winter work Steel wheels are tough, inexpensive and easy to replace, which makes them a practical base for winter sets. Diesel needs cold protection Untreated diesel can start to gel at temperatures well above zero Fahrenheit. DEF freezes too Diesel exhaust fluid freezes at about 12 degrees Fahrenheit, which can limit engine performance until it thaws. Drivers are the first line Short daily checks catch worn wipers, low washer fluid and soft tires before they become roadside calls. Stock every vehicle A basic winter kit in each vehicle turns a breakdown into a delay instead of an emergency. Tires and Wheels for a Working Fleet in Winter Tires are where winter preparation starts for most fleets, because they decide whether a vehicle can stop and turn on cold, wet or icy roads. All-season tires begin to lose grip as temperatures drop and their tread compounds stiffen, so fleets operating in snow country often move service trucks and vans onto dedicated winter tires for the season. Where that is not practical, the minimum is tread with enough depth to clear slush, and pressure checked regularly as temperatures fall. Many fleets simplify the changeover by keeping winter tires on their own wheels. Mounting and balancing tires twice a year for every vehicle adds up quickly in labor and downtime, while a complete winter wheel set can be swapped in a fraction of the time. Steel is the traditional choice for those sets because it is tough, inexpensive and easy to replace if a pothole or curb wins, and for many operators the practical starting point is steel wheels for work trucks and winter beaters . Keeping the paint on steel wheels intact matters, since chips and scrapes are where rust starts. Load ratings deserve a check before any purchase. Work trucks and vans often run near their payload limits in winter, carrying sand, salt, tools and materials, so every wheel and tire should meet or exceed the ratings listed on the vehicle’s door placard. Routes matter as well. Fleets that cross mountain passes or run in regions with chain controls should confirm which traction devices their vehicles need to carry and make sure drivers have practiced fitting them in a dry yard, not for the first time on a dark shoulder in falling snow. Scheduling Preventive Maintenance Before the First Freeze Winter preventive maintenance works best as a planned sweep through the fleet rather than a series of reactions. Batteries come first, because cold weather reduces battery output at the same time engines need more power to start. Testing each battery’s cold cranking amps in the fall, and checking that the alternator is charging properly, finds the weak units while replacement is still a scheduled job rather than a tow. Cooling and heating systems come next. Coolant strength should be confirmed against the manufacturer’s specification, heater cores and blowers checked so crews can keep windows clear, and belts and hoses inspected for cracks that cold weather tends to finish off. Wiper blades and washer fluid round out the list, with winter-rated fluid replacing summer blends before the first frost. In the coldest regions, engine block heaters make a real difference to cold starts, especially for diesel engines. Government Fleet lists them as worthwhile optional equipment for cold climates, and confirming that cords, outlets and timers work before the first deep freeze is far easier than finding a fault at 5 a.m. Tire changeovers are easiest to manage when they are staggered across several weeks rather than crammed into the first snowy week. Fleets that order complete, mounted winter sets through Discounted Wheel Warehouse’s wheel and tire packages can turn each changeover into a straightforward wheel swap during a routine service visit. Recording which set is on which vehicle, along with tread depth at each swap, makes the following season’s planning far easier. Diesel Fleets: Fuel Gelling and DEF in the Cold Diesel vehicles face two cold-weather problems that gasoline vehicles do not. The first is fuel gelling. According to Diesel Army, diesel contains paraffin wax that begins to crystallize in cold weather, with the cloud point for No. 2 diesel around 20 degrees Fahrenheit, and untreated fuel can reach its gel point at about 10 to 15 degrees, where it blocks filters and fuel lines. Winter-blended fuel, blending in No. 1 diesel or kerosene, and anti-gel additives used before the cold arrives all lower that risk, and the same article notes that treating fuel early is far cheaper than an emergency tow. The second is diesel exhaust fluid. Jalopnik reports that DEF freezes at 12 degrees Fahrenheit and expands as it does, which can crack an overfilled tank. A frozen DEF system can put the engine into a reduced-power mode until the fluid flows again, and the same report warns against adding antifreeze to DEF, since it can damage emissions components. Parking in heated space where possible, and never overfilling tanks in winter, avoids most problems. Gasoline vehicles avoid both issues, although keeping their tanks well filled through the winter still gives drivers a margin if they are stuck in traffic or stranded in the cold. Cold-weather risk When it becomes a problem How fleets prevent it Diesel fuel gelling Cloud point around 20°F for No. 2 diesel; gel point around 10 to 15°F Winter-blend fuel, No. 1 diesel blending, anti-gel additive used early Frozen DEF About 12°F Heated parking where possible, no overfilling, no additives in DEF Weak batteries Worse as temperatures fall Fall testing of cold cranking amps and charging systems Low tire pressure After each large temperature drop Gauge checks during pre-trip inspections Driver Checks and Emergency Kits Drivers see their vehicles every day, which makes them the most effective early-warning system a fleet has. Government Fleet recommends that drivers test wipers, check washer fluid level and spray pattern, check tire pressure, and make sure emergency windows and exits open freely. A short, consistent routine at the start of each shift catches most winter problems before they turn into service calls. Commercial vehicles covered by federal motor carrier rules already carry inspection-report requirements, and winter is when a thorough report pays off most. The routine only works if defects reported by drivers are acted on quickly. A simple process, whether that is a paper form, an app or a message to the shop, that turns a driver’s note about a soft tire or a slow crank into a scheduled repair within a day or two keeps small winter problems from growing. Every vehicle should also carry a winter kit. Government Fleet suggests a fresh first aid kit, safety triangles and a charged fire extinguisher, and NHTSA’s winter guidance adds a snow shovel, ice scraper, sand or kitty litter for traction, jumper cables, a flashlight and blankets. Checking these kits at the same time as the fall maintenance sweep keeps them from quietly going missing over the season. Final Thoughts Fleet winter readiness comes down to preparation and routine. Testing batteries, fitting winter tires or complete wheel sets, treating diesel and protecting DEF, and giving drivers a simple daily checklist prevent most of the cold-weather breakdowns that cost fleets time and money. Key Takeaways Schedule a fall sweep that tests every battery, checks coolant and heating, and replaces worn wipers Treat diesel fuel before temperatures approach 20°F and keep DEF from freezing or being overfilled Give every driver a short daily winter checklist and stock each vehicle with a basic emergency kit The fleets that barely notice winter are rarely lucky. They simply did the unglamorous work in October. Frequently Asked Questions How do you prepare a fleet for winter? Start in the fall with a planned maintenance sweep: test batteries and charging systems, check coolant, heaters, belts and hoses, and replace wipers and washer fluid. Move vehicles onto winter tires or complete winter wheel sets where conditions call for it, treat diesel fuel against gelling, and give drivers a daily checklist and an emergency kit for each vehicle. At what temperature does diesel fuel gel? The cloud point of No. 2 diesel, where wax crystals begin to form, is around 20 degrees Fahrenheit, and untreated fuel can reach its gel point at roughly 10 to 15 degrees. At that stage, it can block filters and fuel lines. Winter-blended fuel, No. 1 diesel blending and anti-gel additives lower those temperatures. Does diesel exhaust fluid freeze? Yes. DEF freezes at about 12 degrees Fahrenheit and expands as it freezes, which can crack an overfilled tank. A frozen system can limit engine performance until the fluid thaws. Never add antifreeze or other additives to DEF, since they can damage emissions components, and park in heated space when possible. Should fleet vehicles have winter tires? Fleets that operate regularly in snow, ice or sustained cold benefit from dedicated winter tires, which keep their grip at temperatures where all-season tread compounds stiffen. In milder climates, well-maintained all-season or all-terrain tires with good tread depth may be enough. Mounting winter tires on their own wheels makes the seasonal changeover faster and cheaper. Are steel wheels good for work trucks? Steel wheels suit work trucks well, particularly for winter sets. They are inexpensive, very resistant to cracking and often repairable if bent, and they resist rust as long as the paint stays intact. They are heavier than alloy wheels, but for vehicles that face potholes, curbs and salted roads, durability usually matters more than weight. What should be in a fleet vehicle winter emergency kit? A practical kit includes a first aid kit, safety triangles, a charged fire extinguisher, a snow shovel and ice scraper, sand or kitty litter for traction, jumper cables, a flashlight and warm blankets. Add water and a phone charger, and check every kit during the fall maintenance sweep so nothing is missing when a storm arrives. The post Sustainable Fleet Vehicle Maintenance Tips for the Cold Months Ahead appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News 7 Ways to Bring More Eco-Friendly Practices into Your Healthcare Facility Reading Time: 2 minutes 7 Ways to Bring More Eco-Friendly Practices into Your Healthcare Facility Healthcare facilities have an incredibly important responsibility to protect people’s health, but their operations can also have a considerable environmental impact. From energy-intensive medical equipment to disposable supplies and frequent laundry cycles, everyday healthcare activities consume significant resources. Fortunately, becoming more environmentally responsible doesn’t have to mean compromising patient care or introducing expensive changes overnight. Small, carefully planned improvements can help hospitals, clinics, and care facilities reduce waste, conserve resources, and build more sustainable operations. Make More Sustainable Uniform Choices Healthcare uniforms undergo frequent washing and experience considerable wear, making durability an important consideration when purchasing workwear. When selecting healthcare uniforms for care teams , consider fabric composition, garment longevity, and washing requirements. Natural fibers such as hemp and responsibly sourced cotton may offer environmental advantages, although their overall impact depends on production methods and durability. Choosing well-made uniforms that withstand repeated laundering can also help reduce unnecessary replacements and textile waste. Reduce Unnecessary Single-Use Products Disposable products are essential for infection prevention in many healthcare environments. However, not every item used throughout a facility needs to be discarded after one use . Start by reviewing nonclinical supplies, including administrative stationery, packaging, and breakroom products. Where appropriate, replace disposable items with reusable alternatives, provided they meet hygiene and safety requirements. Clinical waste reduction initiatives should always follow established infection control guidelines. Improve Energy Efficiency Healthcare facilities often operate around the clock, making electricity consumption a significant environmental consideration. Thanks to energy-efficient lighting, smart heating controls, and regular equipment maintenance, there are ways to reduce unnecessary consumption. You could even consider installing motion sensors in suitable low-traffic areas and reviewing ventilation systems to identify potential efficiency improvements. Of course, any changes you make must maintain appropriate temperatures, ventilation, and safety standards for patients and staff. Introduce Better Waste Management Effective waste segregation can prevent ordinary materials from being unnecessarily treated as hazardous clinical waste. Provide clearly labeled disposal containers and train employees to distinguish between recyclable materials, general waste, and regulated medical waste. If you aren’t sure what is going into your bins and whether changes can be made, regular waste audits can identify opportunities to improve recycling rates and reduce disposal costs. Conserve Water Throughout the Facility Healthcare environments use substantial amounts of water for cleaning, sanitation, laundry, and everyday operations. Installing efficient faucets, repairing leaks promptly, and maintaining plumbing systems can reduce unnecessary water consumption. Facilities with on-site laundries might also investigate water-efficient commercial washing machines. Whatever changes are made, water-saving initiatives must never interfere with essential hygiene procedures. Choose Environmentally Responsible Suppliers Sustainability extends beyond what happens inside a healthcare facility. Review purchasing policies and prioritize suppliers that demonstrate responsible manufacturing, reduced packaging, and transparent environmental practices. Ordering frequently used products in appropriate bulk quantities may also reduce packaging and transportation requirements. However, purchasing decisions should balance environmental considerations with product safety, quality, and actual demand. Encourage Staff Participation Employees are often best positioned to identify everyday inefficiencies. Encourage staff to suggest practical improvements, whether that involves reducing unnecessary printing , improving recycling arrangements, or identifying equipment left running unnecessarily. Providing sustainability training and sharing measurable progress can help maintain enthusiasm and encourage long-term participation. Building a Greener Healthcare Environment Creating a more sustainable healthcare facility requires ongoing commitment rather than isolated changes, but starting with achievable goals and measuring their impact can provide the foundation for lasting progress. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Eco-Friendly Pest Control: How Sustainable Methods Save Money and Protect Your Home’s Environment Reading Time: 4 minutes Eco-Friendly Pest Control: How Sustainable Methods Save Money and Protect Your Home’s Environment Readers who follow the restoration stories, pollinator projects, and clean-energy wins that fill this site’s pages already understand a core truth: the choices we make inside our homes ripple outward into the ecosystems we love reading about. Pest control is one of those overlooked household decisions that carries real environmental weight, from groundwater contamination to pollinator die-off, yet it rarely gets the same attention as solar panels or backyard composting. It deserves a closer look, especially now that sustainable pest management has matured into a genuinely competitive, cost-effective alternative to conventional chemical treatments. For homeowners weighing their options, the financial side of this decision matters just as much as the environmental one. In Ohio’s Franklin County suburbs, seasonal shifts bring a predictable parade of ants, spiders, mice, and wood-destroying insects, and local conditions like clay soil and mature tree cover make certain pests more persistent than in other regions. Companies such as Green Shield Pest Pros in Westerville have built service models around integrated, lower-impact treatments precisely because customers are asking for options that protect their families and yards without the long-term costs associated with heavy pesticide use. Understanding where the money actually goes, and where it comes back to you, helps clarify whether the eco-friendly route is worth the initial investment. Why Eco-Friendly Pest Control Costs More Upfront (But Saves Later) Sustainable pest control often carries a higher sticker price per visit than a basic chemical spray, and it is worth being honest about that upfront. Biological treatments, botanical oils, and targeted bait systems require more precise application, more frequent monitoring, and often more skilled technicians than a blanket perimeter spray. That labor and expertise costs more, and homeowners sometimes balk at quotes that run 15 to 30 percent higher than the cheapest conventional competitor in their area. The payoff shows up over months and years rather than on the first invoice. Broad-spectrum pesticides frequently require repeat applications because they kill indiscriminately, wiping out the natural predators that would otherwise keep pest populations in check. Eco-friendly methods, by contrast, work with biological cycles, so homes often need fewer follow-up treatments after the first season. Add in the avoided costs of pesticide exposure, from air filtration to potential health issues, and the higher initial quote starts to look like a reasonable trade rather than a premium. Where Your Money Actually Goes: Prevention vs. Treatment A large share of eco-friendly pest control spending goes toward prevention rather than reactive treatment, and that shift in allocation is where much of the long-term savings originates. Sealing entry points, correcting moisture issues, and installing physical barriers cost money upfront, but they address root causes instead of symptoms. Reactive treatment, the kind most homeowners default to after spotting a problem, tends to be more expensive over a five-year span because it never stops the cycle of reinfestation. The National Pest Management Association reports that 84 percent of homeowners dealt with a pest problem in the past year, which means most families are already paying for pest control in some form, whether through professional services, store-bought products, or property damage. The question is not whether to spend money on pest management but how to spend it most effectively. Prevention-focused spending tends to flatten costs over time, while treatment-only spending creates recurring spikes every time a new infestation takes hold. Metric Figure Global organic pest control market growth $5.4 billion (2025) to $14.1 billion (2034), 11.2% CAGR Biopesticide efficacy against targeted pests 75% to 92%, with Bacillus thuringiensis reaching 85% to 95% larval mortality Residential pest management market share 22.4%, growing at 13.8% CAGR (fastest-growing segment) IPM pesticide reduction vs. baseline (2024 ARMS data) 30.7% reduction in pesticide use, 40.9% mean yield increase Homeowners experiencing a pest problem in past year 84% (NPMA) Integrated Pest Management: The Budget-Smart Approach Integrated Pest Management, commonly shortened to IPM, is the framework behind most eco-friendly pest control programs, and it is built specifically to balance cost against effectiveness. Rather than defaulting to chemical treatment, IPM technicians inspect the property, identify the actual pest and its entry points, and choose the least invasive option that will solve the problem, whether that is a targeted bait, a biological control, or a simple structural fix. This method avoids the waste inherent in blanket spraying, which treats the entire property regardless of where the actual infestation is concentrated. According to this article , Integrated Pest Management programs achieve a 30.7% reduction in pesticide use while delivering a 40.9% mean yield increase, demonstrating that sustainable methods are both environmentally and economically superior to baseline conventional practice. That data comes from agricultural settings, but the underlying principle translates directly to residential pest control: less product applied more precisely produces better outcomes at lower long-term cost. The residential pest management segment is now the fastest-growing part of the broader industry, expanding at nearly 14 percent annually, which suggests homeowners are already voting with their wallets for this smarter approach. Protecting Your Home’s Environment Without Breaking the Bank Protecting the environment immediately around your home does not require abandoning a budget, it requires reallocating spending toward methods that solve problems permanently rather than temporarily. Reducing pesticide runoff protects local waterways and the pollinators that depend on them, while fewer chemical applications inside the home mean better air quality for children and pets. These benefits do not show up as a line item on an invoice, but they represent real value that conventional pest control cannot offer at any price. Homeowners considering a switch should ask providers detailed questions about their methods, request a breakdown of prevention versus treatment costs, and compare multi-year value rather than single-visit pricing. The organic and biological pest control market is projected to nearly triple by 2034, a clear signal that this is not a passing trend but a structural shift in how the industry operates. For anyone already paying attention to the kind of environmental stories featured on this site, choosing pest control that protects both the household budget and the surrounding ecosystem is a small, practical extension of values already in place. The post Eco-Friendly Pest Control: How Sustainable Methods Save Money and Protect Your Home’s Environment appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.titleOriginal: Can Students and Teachers Learn to Trust Each Other in the Age of A.I.?
items.description: «Ανησυχώ αν χρησιμοποιήσω μια παύλα em θα νομίσουν ότι είναι A.I.», είπα στη μαμά μου από εκεί που κάθισα στον πάγκο της κουζίνας, προσπαθώντας να δουλέψω σε ένα από τα δοκίμιά μου στο κολέγιο. Παρά τις διαβεβαιώσεις της για το αντίθετο, δεν πείστηκα. Το μόνο που μπορούσα να σκεφτώ ήταν την περασμένη άνοιξη, όταν η φίλη μου, μια μη μητρική αγγλική γλώσσα που αγαπά να γράφει, μου είπε ότι η ιστορία της…
items.descriptionOriginal: “I ’m worried if I use an em dash they’ll think it’s A.I.,” I told my mom from where I sat at the kitchen counter, trying to work on one of my college essays. Despite her reassurances to the contrary, I wasn’t convinced. All I could think about was last spring when my friend, a non-native English speaker who loves to write, told me that her history teacher accused her of using A.I. to write an essay, his reasoning being that she had included too many “big words.” He didn’t even have a conversation with my friend before giving her a zero. But is her teacher really the villain here? He and his peers have few resources to help them navigate the rise of A.I., and in lots of ways, teachers and students are in the same boat when it comes to figuring out how to adjust to this technological revolution. Somehow, in the process, students have ended up being pitted against teachers. Illustrated by Cloe Moreno One approach would be to rethink homework. Someone recently told me about a professor they know who no longer assigns essays to do at home, and the reasoning makes total sense: The educator said that the idea of walking into his classroom and immediately feeling like he distrusted his students was horrible. He said that he missed being able to look at someone’s work and simply be proud of them, and because of that he was going to have his students write essays solely in class moving forward. While this approach follows a certain logic, it feels detrimental — to students and to teachers — to scrap the whole concept of writing essays outside of class. At the same time, while, at its best, the classroom is a community space full of joyful exploration, how can we create that space if everybody enters it with mistrust? And if teachers come into the classroom automatically distrusting their students, how are we, as students, ever supposed to trust ourselves? Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] I was thinking about exactly these sorts of questions when I discovered the Center for Digital Thriving , a research group based out of the Harvard Graduate School of Education that works with experts, educators and young people to create resources that support teens in their relationship with technology. Based on the principle of the Disability Rights Movement, which is “nothing about us, without us,” the Center for Digital Thriving believes that young people should not simply be spoken about, but should be able to speak, to be given a voice at the table when it comes to things that impact them so immensely. Given that 64 percent of U.S. teens use A.I. chatbots , and almost one in three of those use chatbots daily, it makes sense that research being done about teenagers and A.I. would directly involve them. Illustrated by Cloe Moreno As part of the development of every report, resource guide and lesson plan published by the Center, teenagers are being asked to share their stories and tell experts how A.I. is actually impacting their lives. A core part of this are the teen advisory boards that the Center works with. These are groups of young people who are asked to look at the Center’s research — whether on “ grind culture ” or “ thinking traps ,” and how they’re enhanced by technology — and give their insights and feedback. The Center makes sure that teenagers are directly involved in their process, enabling their research and lesson plans to be genuinely applicable. Educators, in turn, are being given resources for how to deal with A.I. and connect with their students. In one lesson plan, called Align on the Line , teachers are asked to give students a list of activities they might do in that class (for example, a literature class would have steps to writing an essay) and are asked to place them on a spectrum of whether or not they feel the activity could be done with A.I. The spectrum ranges from “totally fine” to “crosses a line,” and allows students and teachers to work with one another, instead of against, to define what they feel is acceptable. Teenagers often say they use A.I. because “it listens.” Just by listening, by being open to hearing what teenagers have to say about their lives, the Center for Digital Thriving is building trust around tech between adults and teens. The goal of the Center is not stopping the use of A.I., but simply creating communities that are informed and on the same page. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime It may seem small, but oftentimes it is the conversations and the communities formed, whether at the kitchen counter or around the seminar table, that begin to chip away reliance on A.I., a dependence which can come from loneliness and a lack of feeling understood. By showing teenagers that they are trusted and that their opinions matter, teenagers may be encouraged to rely on themselves more and A.I. less. Having a space, especially one where research is being done, where teenagers are taken seriously and asked for their insights, is a model for what it can look like to restore young people’s faith in themselves. This article was illustrated by Cloe Moreno, who contributes drawings for podcast episodes and comics that unpack the anxieties and feelings of daily life for This Teenage Life . The post Can Students and Teachers Learn to Trust Each Other in the Age of A.I.? appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.title: Πώς μια ομάδα νεαρών Cherokee έγραψε ιστορία παλεύοντας για ένα ιερό ποτάμι
items.titleOriginal: How a Group of Cherokee Youth Made History Fighting for a Sacred River
items.description: Μια ομάδα κοριτσιών Cherokee, ηλικίας 10 έως 17 ετών, ξεκίνησαν να προστατεύσουν μια σαλαμάνδρα και κατέληξαν να γράψουν νομική ιστορία. Καθοδηγούμενοι από πρεσβύτερους που τους είπαν να ξεκινήσουν με το ίδιο το νερό, οι κόρες NAIWA πέρασαν ενάμιση χρόνο διοργανώνοντας δείπνα στην κοινότητα, συναντώντας τα μέλη του συμβουλίου ένα προς ένα και εμφανίστηκαν, όπως περιέγραψε η ιδρυτής τους, Jasmine Smith, «κουρασμένη, υπερβολική…
items.descriptionOriginal: A group of Cherokee girls, ages 10 to 17, set out to protect a salamander and ended up making legal history. Guided by elders who told them to start with the water itself, the NAIWA Daughters spent a year and a half hosting community dinners, meeting council members one by one, and showing up, as their founder Jasmine Smith described, "tired, overwhelmed, and emotional, sacrificing school breaks and weekends" - until the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians unanimously passed the first all-female-led rights-of-nature resolution in the United States. On the day it passed, the girls carried clay pots of headwaters into the chamber and set the water beside them as the vote was taken; afterward, they carried it back down to the river. The resolution recognizes the Longperson -- the interconnected waterway stretching 790 miles from the Great Smoky Mountains to the Gulf -- as a living entity with inherent rights, and it asks a question that outlasts any single law: "Do we see nature as something we own, or do we view it as something we have the responsibility to protect?" What these young women built was not just policy but a way of belonging to a place -- and a demonstration that a moral compass has no minimum age.

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM You know that moment. The job interview is starting in 30 seconds, and your brain decides now is the perfect time to replay every mistake you’ve ever made. Or you’re halfway through a presentation when a small stumble pulls your focus completely off the material. Performance anxiety doesn’t care who you are. It shows up for professional athletes and first-time public speakers alike, and it always manages to pick the worst possible moment. Cindra Kamphoff has spent her career studying what happens in those moments. She holds a Ph.D. in sport and performance psychology and has worked with organizations including the Minnesota Vikings and USA Track & Field, coaching athletes on managing self-doubt under real pressure. What she’s found is that confidence isn’t a feeling you wait to have before the high-stakes moment. It’s a skill you build, and one you can use in the middle of things going wrong. Kamphoff’s four performance tools Learn, burn, return The instinct when something goes wrong mid-performance is to freeze or spiral. A fumble, a mental blank, a sentence that comes out wrong: whatever it is, Kamphoff has a three-step framework for getting through it. First, learn: ask yourself what you can take from the mistake. The prompt is simple: “Next time, I will ___.” One sentence. You’re done. The point isn’t a full debrief; it’s just a fast pivot so your brain has somewhere to go. Then, burn: choose a physical motion or phrase that tells your brain you’re moving on. A finger snap, saying “that fast,” or, memorably, pretending to flush a toilet. Former Minnesota Vikings wide receiver Adam Thielen used that exact move after a fumble during a 2020 playoff game, then caught a 43-yard pass that helped the Vikings win. Using the same motion every time helps your brain wire a new response, one that interrupts the spiral before it snowballs. Finally, return: bring yourself back with something simple. “You got this. You’re doing the best that you can.” It doesn’t lean “pep-talk”; it’s just more of a reset. Write a power phrase before you need it In 2012, Kamphoff ran a marathon and wrote motivational phrases on her arm so she could read them when self-doubt hit at mile 22. “I’m strong, I’m fast, I’m fit, I’m ready.” It sounds simple, but she wasn’t making things up. She had done the training. She loved running. She had put in hundreds of miles to get there. No amount of mid-race doubt could change any of that, and having the phrases on her arm meant she didn’t have to argue with herself about it. She ran her final four miles faster than any other stretch of the race and won her division. A power phrase starts with “I will,” “I can,” or “I am,” and it’s grounded in something real about what you bring to the situation. Useful questions when building one: How are you at your best? What does that actually feel like? Your answers are usually more solid than what the pre-performance nerves are telling you. Give yourself three goals instead of one Putting everything on a single outcome makes it harder to perform and harder to bounce back if things go sideways. Kamphoff suggests setting gold, silver, and bronze goals instead: a range from your realistic best down to a result you’d genuinely feel okay about. A runner might set winning as the gold goal, a personal best as silver, and a solid finish as bronze. All of those are real targets. None of them require perfection, and having the range means there’s something to run toward even when the gold isn’t happening. The focus shifts to what you can actually do, rather than the outcome you can’t fully control. Fact-check the spiral When negative thinking hits before something high-stakes, Kamphoff recommends three questions: Is that thought true? Is it serving you? And what would be a more useful thing to tell yourself instead? If the thought is “if I don’t ace this interview, I’ll never get another job,” none of those questions take long. The thought isn’t true, it isn’t helping, and a more grounded version might be: “Even if this one doesn’t go the way I want, I know I’m capable, and there will be other opportunities.” It’s a condensed version of what cognitive behavioral therapy calls thought challenging, fast enough to run through in under a minute. The larger point Kamphoff keeps coming back to is that none of this requires being naturally confident. Confidence , in her view, is a decision. “Many times the action of confidence comes before the feeling, and it’s a skill,” she says. You don’t wait until you feel ready. You act, and the feeling tends to catch up. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post How to quiet performance anxiety, according to sport psychology first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Nearly half of U.S. renters and a quarter of homeowners were housing cost-burdened in 2024, meaning they spent more than 30% of their income on housing. Hundreds of thousands of others can afford no home at all. Where can change come from? The question is one of the most complex and pressing of our time, engaging residents, policymakers, and government agencies. But to Kristian Ventura and his co-founders at Actum , the answer is simple. “People want their freedom back, and the best way to do it is to eliminate the biggest burden preventing that, which is rent,” the 26-year-old told Nice News. He established the Los Angeles-based nonprofit, which launched in earnest this year, to put that belief into action: It aims to give away free permanent housing via a lottery system to anyone interested. @universalshelter Spread the good news. ♬ Runaway – Piano Rendition – The Blue Notes & L’Orchestra Cinematique Because the organization doesn’t strictly serve people “in need” by traditional definitions, the leadership team, all friends from high school, had a bit of a hurdle securing its tax-exempt status. The issue lay in the idea that anyone could apply, which made it less clear to the IRS how Actum qualified as a charity, per Ventura. “It’s supposed to be for everyone,” he explained. “That is the point. Homeless individuals are encouraged to apply. Middle class people are allowed to apply.” He added: “Our mission is that universal housing means universal.” Specifically, at least 75% of Actum’s units must be awarded to lottery applicants who make 80% or less of their area’s median income, per its eligibility requirements. The other 25% could technically go to anyone who earns above the median, though Ventura doubts the very wealthy would be interested in living in the basic units the nonprofit plans to purchase and build. As of now, Actum is still in the early stages of fundraising, with a goal of purchasing its first building, likely a duplex or fourplex, when it hits $1 million in donations. The org follows an endowment model for its donations, meaning everything that comes in is immediately funneled into an investment fund, so it can grow at a similar rate to a retirement account. And a live transparency dashboard on its website shows every transaction in real time. Courtesy of Actum Kristian Ventura (upper left), Edmarck Sosa (upper right), and Surya Singh A big part of Actum’s ethos is efficiency. “We actually only run on less than a thousand dollars a year. We have a P.O. box, a website, no paid staff, no pizza parties. We don’t need name tags,” Ventura said, alluding to what he considers wasteful behavior by some charity leaders. “If you actually strip down what a nonprofit has to do operationally, it’s very slim, and that’s what shocks people.” He and his co-leaders, founding members Edmarck Sosa and Surya Singh, met as teens in La Puente, a city in LA’s San Gabriel Valley, and each had come face to face with financial hardships growing up. Singh was born in New Delhi, and would step over children sleeping on the ground outside on his way to school, per Ventura, and Sosa is from Honduras, where his family lived in poverty. Now a rising actor, Ventura bounced around as a child — he and his mother once lived in the garage of a senior care home. After he received a scholarship from the University of Southern California, he had no place to return to during the COVID lockdown; his mom was living out of her car, and his father, who spent years unhoused in San Francisco, died in a government housing unit there in 2023. Kathlyn Almeida “Since we all come from backgrounds of poverty, we take extra efforts to make sure that people who are extremely low income, like single family parents or those living in shelters, know about our lottery,” he explained, adding: “We care about those who sleep in tents, because that’s where the founders come from.” Still, the overarching goal is bigger than just altruism, and the response to Actum’s social media content, which has racked up millions of views, has solidified that they’re onto something. “We’re trying to establish a new standard, which is, it’s technically really unfair for someone to spend 80 hours a week just for a roof over their head. There’s a problem,” Ventura said. “And that’s why we’re going viral, as people understand, ‘Wait, wait, wait. I’m not super, super poor, but I have no time for myself and I feel empty and lonely. So that’s the problem we’re tackling, is this middle class problem as well.” He shared that multiple business owners and other individuals have been reaching out wanting to get involved. “It’s people all coming together with different jobs, different kinds of walks of life, and saying, ‘I believe housing is a human right, and it’s heartbreaking it took this long.’” View this post on Instagram At the time of this writing, Actum had raised around $14,000. “In a way, it’s kind of like a global experiment. Can we actually reach the number that we need to? Can people give to the world they’re going to inherit? It’s a very straightforward model, and it kind of just depends on us. It’s up to us.” RELATED: “They’re Our Neighbors”: Social Entrepreneur Aims to Shift Public Perception of Homelessness in America

items.description: Η διαμάχη ενός εφήβου με τη μητέρα του για τον ύπνο και τη λήθη οδήγησε τον Amit Biligiri, έναν 16χρονο από την Καλιφόρνια, να κάνει μια ερώτηση που μετατράπηκε σε βραβευμένο podcast: γιατί ο εγκέφαλος απορρίπτει μια διάλεξη για τα μαθηματικά του χθες αλλά κρατιέται σε ένα χάρτινο στέμμα πριν από μια δεκαετία; Η απάντησή του, που έχει τις ρίζες του στη νευροεπιστήμη αλλά φθάνει σε κάτι mo…
items.descriptionOriginal: A teenager's argument with his mother about sleep and forgetfulness led Amit Biligiri, a 16-year-old from California, to ask a question that turned into an award-winning podcast: why does the brain discard a math lecture from yesterday but hold onto a paper crown from a decade ago? His answer, rooted in neuroscience but reaching toward something more personal, centers on a memory of sitting across from his 87-year-old great-grandfather in a Burger King in Bangalore, India, both of them wearing flimsy gold crowns, sharing fries. "I don't remember what we talked about," Amit says, "but I remember the salt on the fries, the energy of the room and the way his crown sat slightly crooked on his head." What the science reveals -- that emotion is what gives memories their staying power -- is also what the story quietly demonstrates: that the moments we carry longest are rarely the important ones by any external measure, only the ones in which we felt, without condition, that we mattered to someone. Since finishing the podcast, Amit has found his mother listening to it alone, and she tears up every time.

Αυτό που ανακάλυψε στο para powerlifting δεκαετίες αργότερα δεν ήταν απλώς η αθλητική ικανότητα που ποτέ δεν ήξερε ότι είχε, αλλά η ανάκτηση κάτι που…
items.descriptionOriginal: Julie Dickson grew up loving movement -- bikes, swimming, the easy joy of a body in motion -- until high school sorted everyone into "sporty" or not, and she quietly accepted she belonged to the wrong category. What she found in para powerlifting decades later wasn't just athletic ability she never knew she had, but the reclamation of something her younger self once took for granted: the simple right to belong in sport. "These experiences showed me something my younger self naturally knew but the uniformity of high school made me forget: I was a sporty person." As a participant in the World Dwarf Games, her silver medal in powerlifting mattered not because of the podium, but because it was wholly hers -- earned in a community where competitors cheered each other through disqualifications and everyone was chasing their own personal best, not someone else's defeat. It is a quiet reminder that the environments we move through can either diminish us or restore us to ourselves, and that it is never too late for the latter.

items.title: Η Gen Z σώζει εκατομμύρια σε ιατρικές προμήθειες
