items.description: Στις αρχές Αυγούστου, ένα φορτηγό έφτασε σε μια εγκατάσταση του OhioHealth στο Κολόμπους και πήρε περίπου 30.000 λίβρες μάσκες N95 και ζεστές και κρύες συσκευασίες, όλα συσκευασμένα, σφραγισμένα και σφραγισμένα με ημερομηνίες λήξης ακόμη ένα ή δύο χρόνια έξω. Αν μείνουν μόνες, οι ιατρικές προμήθειες αξίας 250.000 δολαρίων που εκτιμάται ότι θα είχαν πεταχτεί τελικά, θεωρούμενο απίθανο…
items.descriptionOriginal: I n early August, a freight truck pulled up to an OhioHealth facility in Columbus and took roughly 30,000 pounds of N95 masks and hot-and-cold packs, all boxed, sealed and stamped with expiration dates still a year or two out. Left alone, the estimated $250,000 worth of medical supplies would eventually have been thrown away, deemed unlikely to be required before their use-by date. Instead, the pallets were loaded and driven off toward Pittsburgh, the first leg of a journey to an under-resourced clinic on another continent. The operation was part of Project MedBridge , a medical redistribution initiative set up by 16-year-old Ben Kurian, a junior at Olentangy Liberty High School in Powell, Ohio. The idea started, as a lot of good ideas do, at the dinner table. His mother is a nurse practitioner and his family friends are doctors and nurses. Over and over he heard the same uncomfortable fact — every year, big hospitals like OhioHealth and Cardinal Health discard thousands of pounds of good quality supplies simply because they won ’ t be used before their expiration date passes, a problem greatly exacerbated by the pandemic-driven overstock . Ben Kurian (left) and Naman Soni during a Project MedBridge redistribution operation. Credit: Project MedBridge “ These are perfectly usable, sterile supplies, ” Kurian says. “ They don ’ t come out of the box, and yet no one is putting them to use, despite the fact that there are clinics with little-to-no resources in desperate need. ” When he learned that the Carnegie Young Leaders Program funds exactly the kind of social impact idea he had in mind, Kurian started cold-emailing distributors that route surplus overseas, and eventually the Pittsburgh-based nonprofit Brother ’ s Brother Foundation stepped in to handle shipping. Project MedBridge only started this year, but Kurian is far from alone in his desire to curb excess medical waste. Most of the established medical supply redistribution organizations, or MSROs, like Project C.U.R.E. and World Medical Relief (WMR), are staffed full-time by adults operating at industrial scale. But around the country, a quiet network of young people has taken up the same cause: pulling medical surplus out of the waste stream and redirecting it toward people who need it, both in faraway countries and at underserved U.S. clinics. What ’ s striking about this newer wave is that it ’ s run entirely by students, and almost entirely by volunteers — teenagers and Gen Z youth squeezing warehouse shifts in between classes and exams to right a wrong they see unfolding on their own doorsteps. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Each group has found its own way to do it. United2Heal , founded at the University of Michigan in 2007 and run by undergraduates, works hand-in-glove with WMR. Every Saturday, over a hundred members meet up — some arriving by 6 a.m. — to check expiration dates and sort through each shipment. “ Anyone who wants to come volunteer with us can, ” says Leah Beel, president of the nonprofit and a junior majoring in molecular, cellular and developmental biology. The only real limitation, she says, is how many students have cars, as they all carpool to WMR ’ s offices 40 minutes or so from the university. The post Gen Z Is Rescuing Millions in Medical Supplies appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.description: Η Amanda Gl ser-Bligh ονόμασε το δέντρο του δρόμου της Linda -- μια φλαμουριά, οκτώ ετών, που μεγαλώνει έξω από το διαμέρισμά της στο Βερολίνο -- και μια φορά την εβδομάδα τους ζεστούς μήνες, μεταφέρει 20 λίτρα νερό στις ρίζες της Linda. Αυτή η ιδιαίτερη αφοσίωση δεν είναι πλέον ασυνήθιστη: η εφαρμογή ανοιχτού κώδικα Gie den Kiez του Βερολίνου χαρτογραφεί σχεδόν ένα εκατομμύριο δέντρα στους δρόμους ανά είδος…
items.descriptionOriginal: Amanda Gl ser-Bligh has named her street tree Linda -- a linden, eight years old, growing outside her apartment in Berlin -- and once a week through the hot months, she carries 20 liters of water down to Linda's roots. That particular devotion is not unusual anymore: Berlin's open-source Gie den Kiez app maps nearly a million street trees by species, age, and thirst, and 12,000 volunteers now show up with watering cans to tend them alongside city maintenance crews. The project's lead, Anna Mehrl nder, found herself caught off guard by what she discovered: "I was really surprised at just how deeply people care about trees - for many people it's almost like caring for a pet." What the app understood, perhaps before its designers fully did, is that many people already wanted to help and simply needed permission - as Gl ser-Bligh puts it, once you have something "encouraging you, you know it's the right thing to do." At a moment when climate change can feel impossibly large, Berlin found that the distance between despair and action was sometimes just a flight of stairs and a watering can.

items.description: Εδώ ήταν τρεις ξεκάθαροι λόγοι για τους οποίους η Leslie Gomez Rivera απέφυγε την καφετέρια στο λύκειο της στο Μπρούκλιν: Δεν της άρεσε το φαγητό, το δωμάτιο ένιωθε ταραχώδες και υπήρχε ένα στίγμα που συνδέονταν με την κατανάλωση σχολικών γευμάτων. Προτιμούσε τη βιβλιοθήκη, όπου μπορούσε να μιλήσει με φίλους, αν και μερικές φορές αυτό σήμαινε ότι θα πήγαινε εντελώς χωρίς μεσημεριανό γεύμα. Όταν λοιπόν ο Ρίβερ…
items.descriptionOriginal: T here were three clear reasons why Leslie Gomez Rivera avoided the cafeteria at her high school in Brooklyn: She didn’t like the food, the room felt hectic and there was a stigma attached to eating school meals. She preferred the library, where she could talk with friends, although sometimes that meant going without lunch altogether. So when Rivera heard about Youth Food Advocates (YFA), an initiative that trains New York City students to research issues around school food and advocate for changes, she realized she might be able to do something to make the whole situation better. With the help of YFA, the 16-year-old developed a survey and circulated it around Midwood High. She wanted to know what her fellow students liked to eat, what they wanted on the menu, why they stayed away from the cafeteria and what might make them come back. Participants at a Youth Food Advocates leadership training. Credit: Community Food Advocates “I had the answers to [some of the questions],” Rivera recalls, “but I wanted to know what my peers thought.” Around 100 students responded out of roughly 4,000 across Midwood’s two buildings. Their answers complicated the verdict that school lunch was simply bad. Participants singled out popcorn chicken, sauces, fruit and salads as popular items. They also raised concerns about food quality and limited choices, and some wanted more of the foods they ate at home. This was back in late 2020. By then, NYC had already made lunch free for every public school student following years of advocacy that included student organizers from YFA. But free food did not necessarily equate to food students wanted to eat, or a cafeteria where they wanted to spend their lunch period. The post How NYC Students Saved School Lunch appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

Πείτε μας τι έχετε διαβάσει στο info@reasonstobecheerful.world και ίσως το παρουσιάσουμε εδώ. Sunny outlook Πέρυσι, ο συνεισφέρων συντάκτης Peter Yeung ανέφερε σχετικά με τη δυνατότητα αλλαγής του παιχνιδιού της ηλιακής ενέργειας μπαλκονιού — δηλαδή, μικρών ηλιακών συστοιχιών που μπορούν να συνδέσουν…
items.descriptionOriginal: Welcome back to our weekly behind-the-scenes glimpse at what’s getting our team talking. Tell us what you’ve been reading at info@reasonstobecheerful.world and we just might feature it here. Sunny outlook Last year, Contributing Editor Peter Yeung reported on the game-changing potential of balcony solar — that is, small solar arrays that can plug into regular electrical outlets. Now, as Grist reports in a story Peter shared this week, California Governor Gavin Newsom has signed a bill that will allow residents to get on board — and more states could soon follow California’s example. These plug-in solar devices, Grist explains, are a way of “turning homes and apartments into a distributed network of tiny power plants.” Peter says: The balcony solar revolution continues. Light room You know how a squid can change its coloration by revealing or hiding different pigments? That’s the inspiration behind a new type of window panel that “dynamically shades in response to the sun’s rays,” according to a Be Giant story shared by Editorial Director Rebecca Worby. In a typical building, counteracting the heat that enters or escapes through its windows accounts for about a quarter of the energy used. Based on simulations, researchers estimate that one version of these squid-like window panels could lower buildings’ heating use by 75 percent and their total energy use by 43 percent. Becca says: Intriguing — and the artist’s interpretation at the top of the story has James Turrell vibes. What else we’re reading In a warming Arctic, Inuit bear guards protect communities — shared by Rebecca Worby from Grist Women Can Now Assess Their Breast Cancer Risk With the Help of A.I. — shared by Contributing Editor Michaela Haas from the New York Times New York expands free SUNY and CUNY tuition to those with college degrees — shared by Rebecca Worby from News10 ABC In other news… RTBC Founder David Byrne has a new book out this week! If you’re a fan of our journalism, we suspect you’ll also enjoy Sleeping Beauties: Why Good Ideas Go Dormant and How They Wake Up . Publishers Weekly calls it a “wonderful and humbling celebration of the lost and found.” Read an excerpt from the book in Nautilus and pick up a copy wherever books are lent or sold . The post What We’re Reading: California Joins the Balcony Solar Revolution appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.description: B eep. Μπιπ. Μπιπ. Το όργανο παρακολούθησης του καρδιακού παλμού κελαηδάει. Τα νοσοκομεία προσπάθησαν εδώ και καιρό να καταπολεμήσουν το ακουστικό χάος με παθητικές τακτικές - κρεμώντας πλακάκια οροφής που απορροφούν τον ήχο, τοποθετώντας δάπεδα από μαλακό καουτσούκ ή παρακαλώντας το ιατρικό προσωπικό να ψιθυρίζει στους διαδρόμους. Μπιπ. Μπιπ. Μπιπ. Η αρτηριακή πίεση πέφτει. Αλλά το Royal Cornwall Hospitals NHS Trust στο Ηνωμένο Βασίλειο h…
items.descriptionOriginal: B eep. Beep. Beep. The heartbeat monitor chirps. Hospitals have long tried to fight acoustic chaos with passive tactics — hanging sound-absorbing ceiling tiles, laying soft rubber flooring or begging clinical staff to whisper in the corridors. Beep. Beep. Beep. Blood pressure drops. But the Royal Cornwall Hospitals NHS Trust in the United Kingdom has been trying something different. Instead of regarding noise as an inevitable physical nuisance that needs to be muffled, it treats sound as data that can be routed. In 2023, the trust launched the Silent Hospital Pilot Project , a three-year study exploring how to target “alarm fatigue” and noise pollution on hospital wards. As the second phase of the pilot comes to an end, its outcomes have already been so promising that other hospital networks around the U.K. are preparing to follow suit. Beep. Beep. Beep. Oxygen levels dip. Hospital wards are notoriously loud, with continuous background noise on intensive care units , for example, often averaging 50 to 70 decibels (dB), comparable to heavy traffic, and sharp peaks frequently passing 80 to 100 dB, roughly the equivalent of a jackhammer. These levels vastly exceed the World Health Organization’s recommended threshold of 30 dB to be able to rest. BEEP. BEEP. BEEP. BEEP. BEEP. The monitor escalates to an urgent, repeating multi-tone musical sequence engineered to demand immediate human attention. Studies across international health systems reveal that clinical staff encounter hundreds of alarm signals per shift, up to 90 percent of which require no clinical intervention, for example because a patient mistakenly presses the buzzer when they move. The post The Hospital That Silenced the Machines appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .
